title: The impossible dye mixture
prompt: Three columns of a matrix describe the color mixtures three printers can produce. A requested color vector b lies outside their column space. What is true?
options: No printer settings can produce b exactly
The system must have exactly one least-squares solution
The matrix must have a nontrivial nullspace
The columns must be linearly independent
hint: The column space is precisely the set of outputs the columns can combine to make.
explanation: Every output Ax is a linear combination of the columns of A. If b is outside that span, Ax=b has no exact solution. A best approximate color may still exist.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Column Space and Nullspace

title: A hidden knob
prompt: A machine has four adjustable knobs and produces outputs in three measured dimensions. Its 3-by-4 response matrix has rank 3. Can two distinct knob settings produce exactly the same output?
options: Yes; at least one nonzero knob change leaves output unchanged
No; full row rank means every input maps uniquely
No; four knobs and three outputs imply four independent columns
Only if the output is zero
hint: Compare the number of input directions with the number of independent output directions.
explanation: The nullity is number of columns minus rank: 4-3=1. A nonzero nullspace direction can be added to any setting without changing the output.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Solving Ax=0

title: The least-committal two-knob setting
prompt: A sensor reports only the sum of two controls: x₁ + x₂ = 1. Infinitely many settings match the sensor. Which matching setting has the smallest Euclidean norm?
hint: Among points on the line x₁+x₂=1, the closest to the origin lies perpendicular to that line.
explanation: The constraint is a line in the plane. Its point closest to the origin is its perpendicular foot, (1/2, 1/2), whose squared norm is 1/2. The alternatives also satisfy the equation, but their squared norms are 1 or 5.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Left and Right Inverses; Pseudoinverse

title: A dependency in the lab
prompt: A 3-by-3 matrix A has a third column equal to the sum of the first two. What can you conclude about Ax=b?
options: Some b have no solution; any solvable b has more than one solution
Every b has exactly one solution
Every b has infinitely many solutions
No b other than zero has a solution
hint: The columns do not span all of 3D output space, and there is a nonzero null direction.
explanation: The columns are dependent, so the rank is at most 2. In 3D the column space is therefore smaller than the full output space, so some b are unreachable. Dependence also gives a nonzero null vector, which can be added to any solution without changing the output.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Independence, Basis and Dimension

title: The shortest explanation
prompt: A data vector b is approximated by A x-hat, the least-squares fit. Which geometric fact characterizes the best fit?
options: The residual b-Ax-hat is orthogonal to every column of A
The residual is parallel to every column of A
The fitted vector must equal b
The residual has the same length as each column
hint: Think about what would happen if you nudged the fit in any column direction.
explanation: At the minimum, a small change along any column cannot shorten the residual. Thus the residual is perpendicular to the column space: Aᵀ(b-Ax-hat)=0. This condition can hold even when b is not exactly in the column space.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Projection Matrices and Least Squares

title: Projection order matters
prompt: Project v=(1,0) onto the x-axis, then onto the line y=x. Compare that with doing the projections in reverse order. What happens?
options: The results differ: (1/2,1/2) versus (1/2,0)
Both orders give (1,0)
Both orders give (1/2,1/2)
The projections cancel and both give (0,0)
hint: The first projection is a no-op here. The second order changes the vector before the x-axis projection.
explanation: Projecting (1,0) onto the x-axis leaves it unchanged; projecting that result onto y=x gives (1/2,1/2). In the reverse order, projecting onto y=x first gives (1/2,1/2), whose x-axis projection is (1/2,0). Different projections need not commute.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Projections onto Subspaces

title: A projection with a twist
prompt: A matrix P satisfies P²=P, but it is not symmetric. Which statement is guaranteed?
options: P projects onto its column space, though generally not orthogonally
P is an orthogonal projection
P has only eigenvalue 1
P must be invertible
hint: Idempotence means vectors in the image are left alone. Symmetry adds a separate geometric property.
explanation: P²=P makes P an idempotent projection: its image is fixed, and vectors are mapped there. Orthogonal projection additionally requires P=Pᵀ. An oblique projection need not be symmetric.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Projection Matrices and Least Squares

title: The uphill direction
prompt: A symmetric matrix has eigenvalues 4, 1, and -2. You want to minimize xᵀAx over all vectors with length 1. What is the minimum?
hint: For a symmetric matrix, rotate into its orthonormal eigenvector coordinates.
explanation: On the unit sphere, xᵀAx is a weighted average of the eigenvalues, with weights equal to squared coordinates in an orthonormal eigenbasis. The minimum is the smallest eigenvalue, -2.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Positive Definiteness and Minima

title: The misleadingly friendly diagonal
prompt: A symmetric matrix has 1s on both diagonal entries and 2s off the diagonal: A = [[1,2],[2,1]]. Is xᵀAx positive for every nonzero x?
options: No; along (1,-1), it is negative
Yes; both diagonal entries are positive
Yes; symmetry guarantees nonnegative energy
No; its determinant is positive
hint: Try the direction (1,-1), where the off-diagonal terms matter.
explanation: For x=(1,-1), xᵀAx = -2, so the matrix is indefinite despite its positive diagonal. Its eigenvalues are 3 and -1. Positive diagonal entries alone do not ensure positive definiteness.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Symmetric Matrices and Positive Definiteness

title: The negative edge
prompt: A directed graph is encoded with one row of an incidence matrix per edge: -1 at the source, +1 at the destination. For a vector of node potentials, what does multiplying by this matrix produce?
options: Potential difference along each edge
The average potential of each connected component
The number of paths from each node
A list of node degrees
hint: In a row with two nonzero entries, subtract the source value from the destination value.
explanation: The row computes potential at the destination minus potential at the source. A common sign convention reversal flips all differences but preserves the underlying edge-gradient idea. MIT's notes use -1 at the source and +1 at the destination.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Graphs and Networks, Incidence Matrices

title: A matrix that vanishes when squared
prompt: A nonzero 2-by-2 matrix M satisfies M²=0. Which statement must be true?
options: Both eigenvalues are zero, even though M is not the zero matrix
M is invertible, with inverse M
At least one eigenvalue is 1
M must be symmetric
hint: If Mv=λv, then M²v=λ²v.
explanation: For any eigenpair, M²v=λ²v. Since M²=0, every eigenvalue satisfies λ²=0, so both eigenvalues are zero. A nonzero example is [[1,1],[-1,-1]], whose square is zero. Zero eigenvalues do not imply the matrix itself is zero.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

title: The flip that changes volume
prompt: A 3D linear transformation has determinant -1. What is necessarily true about the signed volume of any transformed box?
options: It is multiplied by -1, so orientation flips while volume magnitude is preserved
Its volume is multiplied by 0
Its volume doubles and orientation stays the same
Its volume cannot be determined even in magnitude
hint: The determinant carries both volume scaling and orientation information.
explanation: The absolute determinant is the volume scale factor. Its negative sign means orientation is reversed. Here |det A|=1, so the volume magnitude is unchanged.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Cramer's Rule, Inverse Matrix and Volume

title: Same map, new coordinates
prompt: You represent the same linear transformation in a different basis. What happens to its eigenvalues?
options: They stay the same
They all become zero
They are multiplied by the determinant of the basis matrix
They are preserved only if the new basis is orthogonal
hint: Changing basis re-expresses the same map; it does not alter the map itself.
explanation: The matrices in two bases are similar: B⁻¹AB. Similar matrices share a characteristic polynomial and therefore the same eigenvalues. Their coordinates differ, but the transformation does not.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Change of Basis; Image Compression

title: The long-lived mode
prompt: A matrix has eigenvalues 0.9, 0.5, and -0.2. Repeatedly applying it to a generic vector, which component tends to dominate after many steps?
options: The eigenvector direction for 0.9
The eigenvector direction for 0.5
The eigenvector direction for -0.2
All directions remain equal forever
hint: Repeated application raises each eigenvalue to a power.
explanation: After k applications, an eigenvector component is scaled by λᵏ. The 0.9 mode decays slowest because it has the largest magnitude. The negative mode also alternates sign as it shrinks.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Diagonalization and Powers of A

title: The coin that never settles
prompt: A two-state Markov chain flips state 1 to state 2 and state 2 to state 1 with certainty. Its stationary distribution is (1/2, 1/2). Starting in state 1, what happens to the distribution after many steps?
options: It alternates forever between (1,0) and (0,1)
It converges to (1/2,1/2)
It converges to (1,0)
It becomes undefined after two steps
hint: A stationary distribution exists, but the chain moves deterministically at each step.
explanation: From state 1, the distribution alternates between the two point masses at every step. The stationary mixture (1/2,1/2) remains fixed if used as the start, but this deterministic chain does not converge to it from state 1. A stationary distribution alone does not guarantee convergence; periodicity matters.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Markov Matrices; Fourier Series

title: Compress the noisy image
prompt: An image matrix has singular values 12, 7, 0.2, and 0.1. Keeping only the first two singular-value terms gives what kind of result?
options: A rank-2 approximation that captures the strongest two modes
An exact reconstruction because two singular values are large
A projection onto the last two modes
A reconstruction with rank 4 but half the pixel count
hint: Each singular-value term is one rank-1 component.
explanation: Truncating the singular value decomposition after two terms gives rank at most two and retains the two strongest modes. It is the best rank-2 approximation in the standard least-squares matrix sense, but it does discard information.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Singular Value Decomposition

title: The shape of a matrix
prompt: A rectangular matrix maps a 5D space into a 3D space and has rank 2. What does its singular-value decomposition reveal geometrically?
options: It stretches two orthogonal input directions into two orthogonal output directions; the other three input directions vanish
It rotates all five input dimensions into three equal output dimensions
It has three nonzero singular values because there are three outputs
It must preserve distances in a 2D plane
hint: The right singular vectors are input directions; the left singular vectors are output directions.
explanation: Rank 2 means exactly two positive singular values. Along corresponding right singular vectors, A maps to orthogonal left singular vectors scaled by those singular values. The remaining three input directions lie in the nullspace.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Singular Value Decomposition

title: The singular fit
prompt: A is a tall matrix with dependent columns. You need the least-squares prediction Ax, but many coefficient vectors x fit equally well. What is the most precise statement?
options: The fitted vector Ax is unique, but the coefficient vector x need not be
Neither the fitted vector nor any coefficient vector is unique
The coefficient vector is unique because A has more rows than columns
There is no least-squares minimum
hint: The closest point in a subspace is unique even if its coordinates in a redundant column set are not.
explanation: The projection of b onto the column space is unique, so the fitted value Ax is unique. If the columns are dependent, nullspace directions can be added to any minimizing x without changing Ax.

source.title: MIT 18.06SC: Left and Right Inverses; Pseudoinverse

title: The host knows where the prize is
prompt: A prize is equally likely to be in any of 3 lockers. You pick one. The host, who knows where the prize is, always opens an empty locker you did not pick, then offers you the other closed locker. What is the chance switching wins?
options: It depends on which empty locker the host prefers
hint: Your first pick was wrong in 2 out of 3 cases. When it was wrong, the remaining closed locker must hold the prize.
explanation: If your first choice was correct (probability 1/3), switching loses. If it was wrong (probability 2/3), the host's rule forces the only other unopened locker to contain the prize. Therefore switching wins with probability 2/3. The host's informed, consistent rule matters.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Conditional Probability, Independence, and Bayes' Theorem

title: The two-coin mystery
prompt: One of two coins is selected with equal probability. Coin A has two heads sides; coin B has one head and one tail. You flip the chosen coin and see heads. What is the chance you chose coin A?
hint: A heads observation is twice as likely under A as under B.
explanation: The joint chances are P(A and H)=1/2 and P(B and H)=1/4. Among the 3/4 total chance of heads, two thirds came from coin A. This is a small example of updating a prior by likelihood.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Conditional Probability, Independence, and Bayes' Theorem

title: One of the dice is a one
prompt: Roll two fair dice. Given that at least one shows a 1, what is the chance their sum is 3?
hint: List the 11 ordered outcomes containing at least one 1.
explanation: The eligible ordered outcomes are (1,1) through (1,6), plus (2,1) through (6,1) without double-counting (1,1): 11 total. Two make 3: (1,2) and (2,1). The answer is 2/11.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Exam 1 Practice Questions I

title: The lucky lab coat
prompt: A disease affects 1% of people. A test catches 90% of true cases and is falsely positive for 9% of healthy people. Someone tests positive. Roughly what is the chance they have the disease?
hint: For every 100 people, about one is sick and nine healthy people test positive.
explanation: Out of 10,000 people, about 90 sick people test positive and about 891 healthy people also test positive. So about 90/981, or 9%, of positive results are true positives. A strong-sounding test can still have a low positive predictive value when the condition is rare.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Conditional Probability and Bayes' Theorem

title: Waiting for a double-head
prompt: You flip a fair coin until you see two heads in a row. How many flips do you expect?
hint: Track whether the most recent flip was a head. A tail sends you back to the starting state.
explanation: Let E be the expected flips from the start and F the expected extra flips after one head. E = 1 + (E+F)/2 and F = 1 + E/2, because a tail resets the streak while a head finishes it. Solving gives E = 6. The waiting time for a pattern can exceed its reciprocal probability because failed partial matches cost flips too.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Discrete Random Variables and Expected Value

title: The uncorrelated signals
prompt: Two random signals have zero correlation. Which statement must be true?
options: They are uncorrelated, but they may still be dependent
They are independent
One signal must be constant
Both signals must be Gaussian
hint: Independence implies zero correlation under suitable finite-variance conditions, but does the reverse always follow?
explanation: Zero covariance rules out a linear association, but nonlinear dependence can remain. For example, if X is symmetric about zero and Y=X², their covariance can be zero even though Y is determined by X.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Joint Distributions, Independence, Covariance and Correlation

title: The sum of many tiny quirks
prompt: You average measurements from 400 independent instruments. Each error is centered at zero with standard deviation 2. What is the standard deviation of the average?
hint: Averaging n independent errors shrinks the standard deviation by √n.
explanation: The standard deviation of the sample mean is σ/√n = 2/20 = 0.1. The instrument readings remain noisy, but their average is much more stable when errors are independent and centered.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Central Limit Theorem

title: The bus that does not remember
prompt: A bus arrives according to a Poisson process averaging one bus every 10 minutes. You have already waited 10 minutes. Assuming a constant rate, how long should you now expect to wait?
options: 10 more minutes
0 minutes
5 minutes
20 more minutes
hint: For an exponential waiting time, the distribution is memoryless.
explanation: The exponential distribution has the memoryless property: prior waiting does not change the expected remaining wait when the arrival process has a constant rate. A different arrival process with scheduled or clustered service could behave differently.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Continuous Random Variables and Exponential Distribution

title: The selected winner
prompt: A team tries 20 candidate model variants on the same small validation set, then reports the best score. What is the main statistical danger?
options: Picking the best among noisy scores creates upward selection bias
Averaging candidate scores makes the validation set effectively larger
The best score estimates deployment performance without extra bias
Choosing by validation score does not affect its interpretation
hint: The selection rule itself uses the noisy validation score.
explanation: Even if each candidate's validation score is a noisy estimate, choosing the maximum favors candidates that got lucky. A separate final test set or nested validation is needed for an unbiased assessment of the chosen model.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Exam 2 and Significance Testing

title: The endlessly patient scientist
prompt: A researcher tests a null hypothesis repeatedly as new data arrive, and stops the moment p drops below 0.05. What is the main issue with reporting the final p-value as if they planned one test?
options: The false-positive rate can exceed 5% because the stopping rule uses the results
Nothing; each individual test still uses 0.05
The final p-value becomes a posterior probability
Repeated testing only reduces statistical power
hint: The chance of at least one threshold crossing grows when you keep checking.
explanation: A nominal 5% threshold controls the false-positive rate for a specified test under its assumptions. Repeatedly checking and stopping on a favorable result changes the procedure and can raise the overall false-positive rate. The analysis plan and stopping rule matter.

source.title: MIT 18.05: The Frequentist School of Statistics; NHST I

title: Twenty tiny alarms
prompt: A team tests 20 independent null hypotheses at a 5% significance level, with no correction. If all 20 nulls are true, what is the chance of at least one false alarm?
options: About 64%
Exactly 5%
About 20%
Zero, because the tests are independent
hint: It is easier to compute the chance of no false alarms: 0.95²⁰.
explanation: The chance of no false positives is 0.95^20, about 0.36. Therefore the chance of at least one is about 0.64. Testing many hypotheses raises the family-wise false-alarm chance.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Exam 2 and Significance Testing

title: The lopsided randomized trial
prompt: In a randomized trial, the treated group happens to start with somewhat higher baseline disease severity. A colleague says this proves the treatment allocation was not really random. What is the best response?
options: Chance imbalance can occur; a planned severity adjustment may improve precision
Chance imbalance means assignment failed, so analyze the trial as observational
Adjust only if severity's baseline group-comparison p-value is below 0.05
Drop participants until severity is balanced between groups
hint: Randomization balances groups in expectation across assignments, not perfectly in every sample.
explanation: A valid random assignment can produce a lopsided realized sample by chance. This does not undo the assignment mechanism. A prespecified adjustment for a predictive baseline covariate can improve precision. Selecting covariates by a baseline p-value or deleting participants after seeing imbalance can distort the analysis.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Experimental Design and Statistical Inference

title: The pooled effect disappears
prompt: A treatment helps in both small and large clinics when each clinic is compared separately. Yet the pooled data show worse outcomes for the treatment group. What is the most plausible explanation?
options: The treatment and control groups have different mixes of clinic sizes, which reverses the pooled comparison
A positive effect in every stratum mathematically forces a positive pooled effect
Pooling causes randomization to fail inside each clinic
The result proves measurement error
hint: Think of clinic size as a lurking variable linked to both treatment allocation and outcome risk.
explanation: This is Simpson's paradox. Different proportions of high-risk and low-risk clinics can reverse an aggregate comparison, even when the treatment does better within each stratum. Inspect assignment and standardize over a common clinic mix.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Joint Distributions, Independence, Covariance and Correlation

title: The estimate that fits exactly
prompt: You fit a line with two parameters through exactly two data points with distinct x-values. The residual sum of squares is zero. Does this demonstrate the model generalizes well?
options: No; two fitted observations say little about how a third will behave
Yes; the two points determine one line, so its slope is validated
No; two observations cannot identify slope and intercept
Yes, provided the optimization converged
hint: The same data were used both to choose and judge the fit.
explanation: Two points identify a line, but fitting them does not test its predictions on new data. To assess generalization, use held-out observations or a justified model assumption. A zero residual describes the training points only.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Linear Regression

title: A quiet result is not a clean bill of health
prompt: A small clinical study finds no statistically significant difference between two treatments (p=0.28). The authors conclude the treatments are equivalent. What is missing?
options: A prespecified equivalence margin and an interval narrow enough to fit inside it
A conventional test that fails to reject equal effects
A confidence interval that includes zero but is wide
A follow-up test with a higher p-value
hint: Failing to detect a difference is not the same as showing that any meaningful difference is small.
explanation: A nonsignificant test may simply be underpowered. Equivalence requires defining a scientifically acceptable difference range in advance and showing the data exclude effects outside that range with suitable confidence. A wide interval that includes zero can still include important differences.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Comparison of Frequentist and Bayesian Inference

title: Which model is more likely?
prompt: A coin lands heads 7 times in 10 flips. Compare H₀, which fixes the coin as fair, with H₁, which gives the coin's unknown heads probability a uniform prior. Which model assigns greater probability to this exact data sequence?
options: H₀, because H₁ spreads prior probability across many possible biases
H₁, because it can fit the observed fraction exactly
They assign the same probability because both include 0.7
It cannot be compared without more flips
hint: An alternative that can fit many patterns pays a prior-probability cost for covering all of them.
explanation: H₀ assigns probability 0.5¹⁰ = 1/1024 to this exact sequence. Under H₁, averaging the likelihood over a uniform prior gives the beta integral 1/1320, which is lower. Fitting the observed fraction best is not the same as assigning the greatest integrated probability.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Maximum Likelihood Estimates and Bayesian Updating

title: The two noisy thermometers
prompt: You average two unbiased measurements of the same temperature. Their errors have equal variance and correlation +1. How much does averaging improve the error variance?
options: None; the average has the same error variance as either reading
It halves the variance
It cuts the variance to zero
It doubles the variance
hint: With correlation +1, the errors move in lockstep.
explanation: Equal-variance errors with correlation +1 are identical almost surely. Averaging them therefore leaves the error unchanged. The variance formula for a mean includes covariance terms; the familiar 1/n reduction relies on uncorrelated errors.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Joint Distributions, Independence, Covariance and Correlation

title: A confidence interval for a new patient
prompt: A 95% confidence interval for a population mean is narrow. You need an interval likely to contain one new patient's measurement. Which is usually wider?
options: A prediction interval for one new observation
The confidence interval for the mean
They are always equal
Neither can be computed without knowing the true mean
hint: An individual outcome has both uncertainty in the mean and its own variation around that mean.
explanation: A confidence interval estimates the mean. A prediction interval for a new observation also includes the observation's individual noise, so under the usual model it is wider. A narrow estimate of an average does not imply individual outcomes are tightly clustered.

source.title: MIT 18.05: Confidence Intervals and Linear Regression

title: Find the broken step
prompt: A yeast mutant needs histidine to grow. The pathway is A → B → C → D → histidine. You pulse cells with labeled A, then measure labeled intermediates. Which pattern best supports a block at the B → C step?
options: B accumulates; label in C, D, and histidine stays low.
All pools look wild type, but only labeled histidine stays low.
B stays low while C accumulates, suggesting a block before C.
Labeled B and C both rise, but D and histidine stay low.
hint: Look for the metabolite immediately upstream of the blocked reaction.
explanation: A block in B → C predicts that carbon reaches B but fails to flow efficiently into C and downstream products. Pool sizes and isotope fractions can be affected by feedback and dilution, so this is evidence for a pathway location rather than proof of a single molecular lesion.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 2: complementation and auxotrophy

title: Same gene or same pathway?
prompt: Two recessive yeast mutants each need histidine. The diploid made by mating them still needs histidine. Under the standard complementation-test assumptions, what is the best conclusion?
options: The two lesions are necessarily in adjacent genes because both affect histidine.
They are likely defective in the same functional gene.
A dominant mutation in either strain masks the recessive mutation after mating.
Failure to complement proves both alleles encode a shared protein complex.
hint: Ask whether either parent supplies the function missing in the other.
explanation: Failure to complement means neither allele supplies the missing function in the diploid, which is evidence that the recessive mutations affect the same gene. The conclusion depends on the usual assumptions, such as no unusual interallelic rescue.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 2: complementation

title: The deceptive heterozygote
prompt: A mutant allele produces traits A and B in homozygotes. Heterozygotes show A but not B. What is the best description?
options: Recessive for both, because one trait is absent.
Dominant for both, because one trait appears in heterozygotes.
Dominant for A, recessive for B.
Dominance is fixed for an allele, independent of the trait.
hint: Dominance summarizes what a specified phenotype does in a heterozygote.
explanation: Dominance is defined for a specified phenotype by comparing homozygotes and heterozygotes.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 2: dominance and phenotype

title: The sugar that is not food
prompt: Bacteria express LacZ after exposure to IPTG, even though they cannot break IPTG down. Which inference does this result support?
options: IPTG may stabilize LacZ after synthesis rather than induce its expression.
IPTG may act at the promoter without interacting with a regulatory protein.
IPTG may be converted into a different intracellular signal before affecting LacI.
Inducer recognition can be separated from substrate turnover.
hint: Could a molecule switch a regulator without being metabolized by the enzyme?
explanation: A gratuitous inducer activates expression without serving as the enzyme's substrate. This separates the regulatory signal from chemical turnover and undermines a template-like explanation of induction.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 16: lac regulation

title: The constitutive mystery
prompt: A lac-system mutant expresses beta-galactosidase with or without inducer. You add a wild-type copy of LacI, and inducibility returns. What does that most strongly suggest?
options: The original defect was a recessive, trans-acting loss of functional repressor.
The reporter is constitutively active, so extra LacI reduces its output by changing lacZ copy number.
A weak operator defect may be partly overcome by excess LacI, so dosage controls should be checked.
The F plasmid altered lactose uptake, which alone restores inducibility.
hint: A diffusible wild-type product can rescue a repressor defect.
explanation: Wild-type LacI supplied from elsewhere can repress the mutant operon, which supports a trans-acting loss-of-function repressor allele. A cis operator mutation would affect only the linked DNA copy and would not be repaired by making repressor elsewhere.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 16: dominance and lac regulation

title: A mutant repressor with bad manners
prompt: A mutant LacI is constitutive and remains dominant when wild-type LacI is added. Biochemistry confirms that mutant and wild-type subunits co-assemble, and mixed complexes bind operator poorly. What mechanism best fits?
options: The mutant protein is produced at higher levels and outcompetes wild type without forming mixed complexes.
Mutant subunits poison mixed repressor complexes.
A cis operator mutation makes the separate wild-type operon constitutive in trans.
A gain-of-function LacI that binds inducer more tightly should make expression constitutive.
hint: Consider what a mutant subunit can do inside a multimer.
explanation: A multimeric repressor can be disrupted by a dominant-negative subunit that coassembles with wild-type subunits. This yields a trans-acting dominant phenotype even though many simple loss-of-function LacI alleles are recessive.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 16: dominant LacI mutants

title: DNA site or diffusible factor?
prompt: A constitutive lac phenotype stays with the linked structural gene in a cis/trans test. What is the strongest inference?
options: A trans-acting activator defect should follow its protein product, not reporter DNA.
A diffusible LacI defect should also affect an unlinked reporter.
The lesion is likely a local DNA control site, such as the operator.
A cis result proves a diffusible repressor can affect only one reporter.
hint: Does the effect follow a DNA molecule or a product that can diffuse?
explanation: A cis-only effect tracks the linked DNA copy, which points to a local regulatory site. A mutation in a diffusible repressor can affect an operon in trans.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 16: cis/trans tests

title: The two-switch inversion
prompt: Lactose-pathway expression rises after lactose appears. In a simple lac model, why can the inducer have a net positive effect even though it inhibits a regulator?
options: It blocks LacZ catalysis, directly signaling the promoter to make more enzyme.
It activates an unrelated activator that overcomes lac repression.
It inhibits RNA polymerase, which increases transcription.
It inhibits a repressor, and the repressor normally inhibits transcription.
hint: Follow the sign of each regulatory link.
explanation: Inhibiting a negative regulator removes repression. The two negative links yield a net positive effect on expression, a useful example of sign logic in regulatory networks.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 16: the lac operon

title: Why score the sons?
prompt: A researcher maps two X-linked markers in flies by scoring male offspring from a cross. Why can this make the marker combinations easier to interpret?
options: Each son has one X chromosome, so the inherited maternal X haplotype is not masked by a second X allele.
Scoring sons shows whether the maternal markers recombined during male meiosis.
Sons inherit their sole X from their father, exposing paternal recombination.
The Y chromosome makes recessive X alleles dominant through dosage compensation.
hint: How many X copies does a typical male offspring have, and where did it come from?
explanation: A male fly is hemizygous for its X chromosome, inherited from its mother, so the alleles on that X can be read from phenotype without a second X-linked allele masking them. The method improves scoring; it does not itself increase recombination.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 7: test crosses and mapping

title: The 50% ceiling
prompt: Two loci produce 50% recombinant progeny in a test cross. What can this result tell you about their physical relationship?
options: No crossovers occurred, so half the offspring appear recombinant by chance.
They must be unlinked, since linked genes cannot yield 50% recombinants.
They may be unlinked or far apart on one chromosome; this result cannot distinguish the cases.
They are linked exactly 50 cM apart.
hint: Multiple crossovers can hide themselves in the final marker pattern.
explanation: Unlinked loci assort to give about half recombinant combinations. Distant linked loci can also approach that fraction because multiple crossovers, including even numbers, can restore parental marker combinations. Thus 50% is a ceiling for this simple measurement, not a precise map distance.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 7: recombination mapping

title: The rarest offspring
prompt: In a three-marker cross, the two most common offspring classes are parental and the rarest pair are double crossovers. How can the rare pair reveal gene order?
options: The rare classes often mark double crossovers, but viability can distort their frequency.
The locus with the lowest single-interval recombination rate must be in the middle.
The middle marker switches in the rare classes; the outside markers stay parental.
The commonest class names the middle gene without comparing haplotypes.
hint: A double crossover restores the outside-marker arrangement but flips the middle marker.
explanation: A double crossover exchanges the middle segment twice. Comparing those rare classes to parental haplotypes reveals which locus lies between the other two. This is a qualitative order clue, not a count-only shortcut.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 7: three-factor crosses

title: The hidden second crossover
prompt: In a three-point cross, the observed double-crossover count is much lower than expected if crossovers in adjacent intervals were independent. What does this suggest?
options: A low count shows that one of the two marker intervals is not linked.
The deficit proves the double-recombinant offspring were misclassified.
Positive interference means crossovers in adjacent intervals occur more often together than expected.
A crossover in one interval reduces the chance of another nearby crossover.
hint: Compare observed double crossovers with the product of the two single-interval rates.
explanation: Fewer double crossovers than expected under independence is positive crossover interference: one crossover reduces the probability of another nearby one. Check viability and scoring before attributing the deficit to interference.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 7: three-factor crosses

title: When a useful allele is lethal
prompt: A new mutation is lethal in a haploid yeast cell. Which experiment can still help classify whether a wild-type copy complements it?
options: Score a viable diploid carrying both mutant and wild-type alleles.
If a heterozygote survives, the allele is dominant in every tissue.
A surviving diploid proves recessivity even without scoring its phenotype.
A diploid test cannot reveal recessivity because both homologs are expressed.
hint: Dominance is defined by a heterozygote phenotype when that comparison is possible.
explanation: The diploid assay compares mutant and wild-type alleles in one cell. If the phenotype is rescued, the mutant effect is recessive for that phenotype; the lethal haploid alone does not establish dominance.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 2: dominance tests

title: One pathway, two rescue profiles
prompt: Mutant M1 grows when supplied with intermediate C or final product H. Mutant M2 grows with H but not C. In pathway A → B → C → D → H, where are the likely blocks? Assume supplements enter the cells and can bypass upstream blocks.
options: Both mutants must block the last step because H rescues both.
M1 blocks production of C or an earlier step; M2 blocks a step between C and H.
M1 blocks a step after C; M2 blocks a step before C.
M1 blocks a step after H; M2 blocks a step before C.
hint: A downstream intermediate can bypass an earlier block; a later block needs a later supplement.
explanation: C can bypass M1's block, placing it upstream of C under these assumptions. C cannot rescue M2 but H can, placing its block between C and H. This brackets pathway position without identifying a particular gene.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 2: auxotrophy and pathway logic

title: The missing phenotypes
prompt: A trait-causing allele appears in only 60% of carriers in one strain background, but in nearly all carriers after crossing into another background. What is the best interpretation?
options: A 60% penetrance result means 40% of carriers are heterozygous and 60% homozygous.
The allele must have lower expressivity, meaning every carrier shows a milder version of the trait.
Incomplete penetrance in the first background.
The allele changes chromosomal position in most carriers.
hint: Separate carrying the allele from showing the phenotype.
explanation: Penetrance is the fraction of individuals with a genotype who show the associated phenotype. A background or environment can alter penetrance without changing the allele sequence.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lecture 2: incomplete penetrance

title: Competitive inhibitor, same Vmax
prompt: An inhibitor increases the apparent Km but leaves Vmax unchanged. What pattern best explains this?
options: Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax while leaving Km unchanged.
Mixed inhibition shifts apparent Km and lowers Vmax, depending on binding preference.
Uncompetitive inhibition lowers both apparent Km and Vmax in the simple model.
Competitive inhibition raises apparent Km; Vmax stays fixed.
hint: Think about whether high substrate can recover the same plateau.
explanation: For a simple competitive inhibitor, substrate and inhibitor compete for free enzyme. High substrate can restore the same asymptotic rate, while more substrate is needed to reach half-maximal velocity.

source.title: MIT 7.05 course calendar: Lecture 11, enzyme kinetics; Lecture 21, glycolysis regulation

title: Same Kd, different Km?
prompt: A mutant enzyme has the same equilibrium dissociation constant Kd for substrate as wild type, but its kcat is much lower. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Km can change because it includes kinetic rates; Kd describes equilibrium binding.
Km must equal Kd in both enzymes, so it cannot change.
A lower kcat proves equilibrium substrate binding is weaker.
The enzyme equilibrium constant for the overall reaction must have changed.
hint: Km and Kd are equal only under a limiting kinetic assumption.
explanation: For E + S ⇌ ES → E + P, Km=(koff+kcat)/kon while Kd=koff/kon. A change in kcat can change Km even if Kd is unchanged; kinetic Km is not generally a pure affinity constant.

source.title: MIT 7.05 course calendar: enzyme chemistry, catalysis, and kinetics

title: The uncompetitive signature
prompt: An inhibitor binds only after substrate has bound. In the simplest kinetic model, what signature is expected?
options: Mixed inhibition can shift apparent Km in either direction while lowering Vmax.
Both apparent Km and Vmax decrease.
Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax while preserving Km.
Competitive inhibition raises apparent Km while preserving Vmax in the simple model.
hint: The inhibitor removes ES from the productive pool, and binds ES selectively.
explanation: Uncompetitive inhibitor stabilizes or traps the enzyme-substrate complex. This lowers both the apparent Km and Vmax in the classic scheme; inhibition depends on substrate-bound enzyme being present.

source.title: MIT 7.05 course calendar: Lecture 11, enzyme kinetics; Lecture 21, glycolysis regulation

title: Why couple ATP hydrolysis?
prompt: A biosynthetic step has positive ΔG under cellular conditions. Coupling it to ATP hydrolysis can make the net process proceed when:
options: ATP use in the same cell makes any positive-ΔG step favorable.
ATP hydrolysis lowers the biosynthetic activation barrier even when the reactions are uncoupled.
The sum of the coupled reaction free-energy changes must be negative.
The reactions can couple only if their equilibrium constants match.
hint: Free-energy changes add for reactions that are chemically coupled.
explanation: Coupled reaction free energies are additive. The overall process is favorable if the sum is negative; ATP hydrolysis occurring nearby but independently does not pull the other reaction along.

source.title: MIT 7.05, Lecture 19: bioenergetics and introduction to pathways

title: The enzyme arms race
prompt: You measure a reversible reaction starting once from mostly A and once from mostly B. Adding tenfold more enzyme speeds both runs. Which result would show the enzyme changed kinetics without changing thermodynamics?
options: The A-start run reaches a different final ratio from the B-start run.
More enzyme makes only the forward reaction faster and permanently raises B at equilibrium.
More enzyme changes the measured equilibrium constant in proportion to enzyme concentration.
Both runs reach the same final A:B ratio, but reach it sooner with more enzyme.
hint: Compare the final ratio with the time needed to reach it.
explanation: A catalyst accelerates forward and reverse reactions but does not change their equilibrium ratio. Starting from either side is a useful check that the system converges to the same equilibrium; changing enzyme amount should alter the time course, not the endpoint.

source.title: MIT 7.05, Lecture 19: bioenergetics and introduction to pathways

title: The bottleneck moves
prompt: A pathway is at steady state. You greatly increase enzyme 1, but pathway flux barely changes. What is the best next thought?
options: Another step or substrate supply may limit flux in this state.
An unchanged metabolite pool proves its flux did not change.
At steady state, increasing an enzyme must increase flux in direct proportion.
All pathway enzymes must be saturated when metabolite levels are stable.
hint: A pathway's control can be distributed and can shift after perturbation.
explanation: Steady state only means concentrations are not changing much over the observation window. Flux control can be distributed across steps and can depend on substrate supply, product removal, and feedback.

source.title: MIT 7.05, Lecture 21: glycolysis regulation and enzyme kinetics

title: Oxygen changes the fermentation plan
prompt: In the 7.05 yeast scenario, glucose is being fermented to ethanol and engineered lactate. Oxygen is then supplied, and the cells can respire. What change is expected under the course question's assumptions?
options: Oxygen is a direct substrate for lactate dehydrogenase, so lactate production rises.
Respiration shifts pyruvate away from fermentation, so both products fall.
Ethanol falls but lactate must rise because both pathways compete for the same pyruvate.
Oxygen inhibits the glycolytic pathway at its first step, stopping all glucose use.
hint: Track pyruvate's competing fates and how respiration restores oxidized electron carriers.
explanation: For the yeast model specified in the MIT exam, oxygen favors pyruvate oxidation through the citric-acid cycle and regenerates NAD+ and FAD through oxidative phosphorylation. This reduces the need to use lactate or ethanol production to rebalance redox. The conclusion is conditional on the stated organism and pathway assumptions, not a universal rule for every cell.

source.title: MIT 7.05, Exam 3 solutions: fermentation and oxygen

title: Keep the cycle from running dry
prompt: Yeast grow on ethanol as their carbon source. A mutant lacking the glyoxylate bypass grows poorly, even though it can make acetyl-CoA from ethanol. Why?
options: Ethanol cannot be oxidized to acetyl-CoA unless glucose is present.
The bypass is the only route that converts oxygen into ATP.
The bypass conserves acetyl-CoA carbon to replenish four-carbon intermediates.
The bypass supplies the carbon atoms of NADH, which otherwise cannot be recycled.
hint: Acetyl-CoA adds two carbons, but a cycle also needs an acceptor pool.
explanation: The glyoxylate cycle bypasses decarboxylating TCA steps and lets microbes and fungi use two-carbon substrates to replenish four-carbon intermediates. This supports continued TCA function and biosynthesis from ethanol-derived acetyl-CoA.

source.title: MIT 7.05 Exam 3 solutions: ethanol oxidation and glyoxylate cycle

title: A redox favor for yeast
prompt: Anaerobic yeast convert ethanol to more acetate after propionate is added. Propionate is reduced to propionaldehyde. Which link best explains the observation?
options: Propionate converts NADH to NADPH, which ethanol oxidation uses instead.
Propionate reduction consumes NADH and therefore removes the oxidized cofactor needed for ethanol oxidation.
Propionate can increase acetate only by donating its carbon skeleton.
Propionate reduction consumes NADH and regenerates NAD+ for ethanol oxidation.
hint: Track where the electrons go, then ask which oxidized cofactor ethanol oxidation needs.
explanation: Reducing propionate to propionaldehyde consumes NADH and regenerates NAD+. The regenerated NAD+ can accept electrons during ethanol oxidation toward acetate. This is an indirect redox coupling through a shared cofactor, rather than direct electron transfer from ethanol to propionate.

source.title: MIT 7.05, Exam 3 solutions: fermentation, cofactors, and anaplerosis

title: Oxygen isotope detective
prompt: You feed cells glucose labeled with 13C and later detect 13C in CO2. What does this result establish?
options: Glucose carbon reached a CO2-releasing step; tracing alone cannot localize it.
The labeled carbon passed through oxidative decarboxylation in the TCA cycle.
The labeled CO2 proves oxidative phosphorylation generated ATP from that carbon.
The cell respired rather than fermented the labeled glucose.
hint: A label reports atom fate, not the whole pathway story.
explanation: CO2 can arise from oxidative decarboxylation or from pyruvate decarboxylase during ethanol fermentation. Label in CO2 establishes carbon release as CO2, but does not distinguish respiration, fermentation, route, or ATP yield.

source.title: MIT 7.05 Exam 3 solutions: fermentation and CO2 release

title: A reaction can run uphill in standard conditions
prompt: For A ⇌ B, ΔG° is +5 kJ/mol. In a cell, [B]/[A]=0.1. Take RT≈2.5 kJ/mol. What is the sign of ΔG for A→B?
options: Positive: the concentration term is always added as a positive number.
Negative: RT ln(0.1)≈−5.8, so ΔG≈−0.8 kJ/mol.
Zero: any enzyme-catalyzed reaction is at equilibrium.
Positive: a positive ΔG° fixes direction regardless of concentrations.
hint: Use ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, with Q=[B]/[A].
explanation: ΔG=ΔG°+RT ln Q. Here RT ln(0.1)≈2.5×(−2.3)=−5.75 kJ/mol. Adding +5 gives about −0.75 kJ/mol, so the forward direction is favorable under these concentrations.

source.title: MIT 7.05, Lecture 19: bioenergetics and introduction to pathways

title: Two sites, one ligand pool
prompt: A receptor has two identical, independent ligand-binding sites. At equilibrium each site is occupied with probability 0.5. What fraction of receptor molecules should have exactly one ligand bound?
options: 100%; every receptor must have its average occupancy.
75%; that is the probability at least one site is occupied.
50%; either site can be the single occupied one, so 2×0.5×0.5.
25%; that is the probability one specified site is occupied.
hint: Count the two mutually exclusive ways to have exactly one occupied site.
explanation: For independent sites, probability of exactly one bound ligand is 2θ(1−θ). At θ=0.5 this is 0.5. The 0.75 value is probability of at least one ligand, while 0.25 is probability both sites are occupied.

source.title: MIT 7.05 course calendar: hemoglobin allostery and enzyme kinetics

title: Dilute enzyme, same chemistry
prompt: You double enzyme concentration while holding substrate at a saturating level and all other conditions fixed. Under Michaelis-Menten assumptions, what changes?
options: Vmax is unchanged because substrate concentration is fixed.
Km halves because the same substrate is shared among more enzyme.
kcat doubles because more enzyme molecules are present.
Vmax doubles; kcat and Km remain unchanged.
hint: Vmax depends on total enzyme; kcat is per enzyme molecule.
explanation: At saturating substrate Vmax=kcat[Et]. Doubling total active enzyme doubles Vmax. Turnover per enzyme and the substrate concentration giving half-maximal rate remain unchanged.

source.title: MIT 7.05 course calendar: enzyme kinetics

title: Uncoupling versus plugging ATP synthase
prompt: A mitochondrion has substrate and oxygen. An uncoupler raises oxygen consumption while ATP output falls. An ATP-synthase inhibitor instead lowers oxygen consumption. Which explanation fits?
options: Uncoupling dissipates Δp; blocking ATP synthase builds it and slows respiration.
Oxygen use must fall in both cases because ATP synthesis is required for electron transfer.
The uncoupler stimulates ATP synthase, while the inhibitor makes the gradient larger and speeds respiration.
Both treatments directly inhibit electron transfer, but the uncoupler increases measured oxygen use by binding oxygen.
hint: One treatment dissipates the gradient; the other prevents protons flowing through ATP synthase.
explanation: An uncoupler allows proton re-entry without ATP synthesis, dissipating proton-motive force and relieving respiratory back-pressure. Blocking ATP synthase prevents proton return, so the gradient builds and electron transport usually slows. Assume substrate and oxygen are not limiting.

source.title: MIT 7.05 Exam 4 solutions: respiratory proton pumping and ATP synthesis

title: Allostery with a plot twist
prompt: An effector binds away from the active site and shifts a sigmoidal enzyme curve leftward. What does that show most directly?
options: A left shift proves the effector raised Vmax, because Km and Vmax always change together.
The enzyme responds at lower substrate; Vmax need not change.
The effector may change enzyme abundance over time, but an acute binding result alone does not establish that.
Allosteric binding must occur at the active site if the curve shifts.
hint: Left shift and vertical plateau are separate features of a response curve.
explanation: A left shift indicates that less substrate is needed for a given fractional response. Whether Vmax changes is a separate question, and allosteric regulation need not involve active-site competition.

source.title: MIT 7.05, Lecture 21: glycolysis regulation and enzyme kinetics

title: An isotope is diluted
prompt: Labeled glutamine supplies carbon to a metabolite, but the product's labeling fraction is lower than expected. Which explanation is plausible?
options: A small labeled fraction means glutamine uptake stopped.
Low enrichment alone proves net glutamine flux fell.
Unlabeled inputs can dilute enrichment despite glutamine flux.
Isotopic enrichment equals absolute pathway flux whenever labeling is at steady state.
hint: Label fraction is not identical to total flux when pools mix.
explanation: Multiple sources, exchange, and pool sizes can dilute isotopic enrichment. A low labeling fraction alone does not mean low total pathway flux or zero glutamine contribution.

source.title: MIT 7.05 General Biochemistry, Exams 3 and 4: metabolism

title: Design a flux experiment
prompt: You suspect enzyme E controls pathway output, but expression and steady-state metabolite levels are noisy. Which experiment gives the most direct causal evidence?
options: Perturb E once and infer flux from transcript abundance only.
mRNA correlation across tissues establishes causal flux control.
One maximal overexpression and a metabolite pool estimate control.
Graded E perturbation plus tracer flux and uptake controls.
hint: A graded perturbation plus a flux readout tests control directly.
explanation: A graded, controlled perturbation can estimate how pathway flux responds to E activity. Tracer-based flux measurement distinguishes flow from pool size; uptake, growth, and off-target effects remain important controls.

source.title: MIT 7.05, Exam 3 solutions: fermentation, cofactors, and anaplerosis

title: Label moves. Nothing accumulates.
prompt: A closed, reversible A ⇌ B reaction is at equilibrium. You label a few A molecules without changing the total concentrations. Label later appears in B, while both pool sizes stay constant. Does the label transfer prove a net A-to-B flux?
options: No. Forward and reverse fluxes can balance while labeled molecules exchange.
Yes. Isotope transfer measures net flux rather than molecular exchange.
No. Equilibrium requires every enzyme molecule to be inactive.
Yes. A constant B pool proves that B is being exported from the closed system.
hint: Distinguish the rates in each direction from their difference.
explanation: At dynamic equilibrium, forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, so net flux is zero. Molecules still interconvert. Isotope labels can redistribute without a change in total A or B; tracer exchange alone does not establish net pathway flow.

source.title: MIT 7.05: Bioenergetics and Equilibrium

title: A rate comparison that changes with substrate
prompt: At a fixed inhibitor concentration, you measure initial rates with and without inhibitor across substrate concentrations. Fractional inhibition is largest at low [S] and falls toward zero as [S] rises. Which model best fits?
options: Uncompetitive inhibition: substrate prevents inhibitor binding to free enzyme.
Competitive inhibition: fractional inhibition falls as substrate increasingly outcompetes inhibitor.
Pure noncompetitive inhibition: high substrate restores the uninhibited rate.
Irreversible inhibition: substrate concentration determines how much enzyme is permanently lost.
hint: For a pure competitive inhibitor, extra substrate should counter its effect.
explanation: Competitive inhibition can be overcome by high substrate, so fractional inhibition falls as [S] increases. Pure noncompetitive inhibition lowers Vmax even at high [S], while uncompetitive inhibition requires ES and is not outcompeted in this way.

source.title: MIT 7.05, Lecture 21: glycolysis regulation and enzyme kinetics

title: Pooling can mimic inbreeding
prompt: Two equally sized, noninterbreeding populations are each in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. Their A-allele frequencies are 0.8 and 0.2. What heterozygote fraction do you expect after pooling their genotypes?
options: 0.25; the pooled population has p²+q² homozygotes.
0.50; use the pooled allele frequency p=0.5 in 2pq.
0.32; average the subpopulation heterozygote fractions 2pq.
0.64; average the subpopulation A-allele frequencies and square the result.
hint: Combine two independently sampled gametes.
explanation: Each subpopulation has heterozygote fraction 2(0.8)(0.2)=0.32. Pooling does not create mating between the groups. The pooled allele frequency is 0.5, whose Hardy-Weinberg prediction would be 0.5; the apparent heterozygote deficit caused by pooling is the Wahlund effect.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lectures 25-27: population genetics

title: An apparent selection signal
prompt: A genotype is overrepresented in a sample from a city compared with a national sample. What is the most important first caution?
options: After ancestry matching, a frequency difference establishes selection rather than drift.
Any frequency difference proves local selection rather than drift.
A city-national difference proves genotyping error.
Ancestry composition or sampling could create the contrast; match groups first.
hint: A frequency contrast can mix biology with who was sampled.
explanation: Population structure can produce frequency differences between samples, even when no selection acted on the trait. Sampling design and ancestry matching matter before attributing a difference to a selective force.

source.title: MIT 7.03 Genetics, Lectures 25-28: population genetics and human polymorphisms

title: A hill with two doors
prompt: A lab script stores one measurement per day. The array rises strictly up to one day, then falls strictly; the peak may be at either endpoint. Which strategy finds a peak in logarithmic time?
options: Compare the midpoint with its neighbors; if it is not a peak, recurse toward the larger neighbor.
Compare the two endpoints and search toward the larger one.
Run binary search for the maximum as if both halves were sorted.
Scan all values, which guarantees a peak but takes linear time.
hint: The sign of one adjacent difference tells you which side still has an ascent.
explanation: If the middle value is smaller than its right neighbor, some peak lies to the right; otherwise a peak lies at or to the left. Repeating halves the search interval, including the endpoint cases.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 01: Introduction and Peak Finding

title: The almost-sorted archive
prompt: A sorted archive has a billion entries. One target is either present once or absent. Which search makes a logarithmic number of comparisons?
options: Scan sequentially; this uses O(n) comparisons in the worst case.
Build a hash table; queries are expected O(1), after O(n) preprocessing.
Compare the midpoint and discard the half ruled out by sorted order.
Use interpolation search, which is always logarithmic on sorted data.
hint: Every comparison should rule out half of what remains.
explanation: Binary search keeps an interval known to contain every possible answer and halves its size each step, taking about 30 comparisons for a billion entries. Sorting is a prerequisite, not part of this lookup cost.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 01: Introduction and Peak Finding

title: The missing middle
prompt: The full run is known to contain every integer from 700 to 729 exactly once, but one ID is missing. The stored array has 29 sorted IDs. Which strategy finds the missing ID in logarithmic time, including when the missing ID is an endpoint?
options: Check adjacent IDs from 700 upward until a gap appears.
Binary-search the first index i where A[i] differs from 700+i.
Compute the expected sum, then scan for an ID that balances it.
Hash the IDs, then test all 30 possible values.
hint: Compare array position i with the value 700+i.
explanation: For each index i before the gap, A[i] = 700+i. Starting at the gap, A[i] exceeds that expected value, including when the missing value is 700. Binary-search the first index where the equality fails; if none fails, 729 is missing.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 07: Counting Sort, Radix Sort, and Lower Bounds

title: Two reports, same day
prompt: Two sorted lists of patient IDs must become one sorted list. What is the key step that makes merge sort efficient?
options: Insert each item from one list at its binary-search position in the other; comparisons are logarithmic but shifts may be linear.
Compare the current fronts, emit the smaller, and advance that list.
Concatenate the lists and comparison-sort all entries in O(n log n).
Alternate entries from the two lists, then repair each out-of-order pair.
hint: Once a front item loses, nothing later in that list can beat the other front.
explanation: The two lists each expose their smallest remaining item. Repeatedly choosing the smaller front costs linear time in their combined length; the full divide-and-merge recurrence yields O(n log n).

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 03: Insertion Sort and Merge Sort

title: Stable sorting, in the right order
prompt: Records need timestamp as the primary key and assay name as the tie-breaker. You have a stable sort and want to use two passes. What should happen first?
options: Stable-sort by timestamp, then stable-sort by assay name.
Stable-sort by assay name, then stable-sort by timestamp.
Use an unstable sort by timestamp, then stable-sort by assay name.
Stable-sort by timestamp only; the earlier assay order will appear automatically.
hint: A later stable pass can reorder the major key while preserving ties from an earlier pass.
explanation: A stable sort by the secondary key first, then a stable sort by the primary key, leaves records timestamp-sorted while retaining assay-name order within timestamp ties.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 03: Insertion Sort and Merge Sort

title: A patient queue
prompt: A clinic repeatedly asks for the highest-priority waiting case and occasionally adds a new one. Which structure is designed for fast insertions and extraction of the maximum?
options: A max-heap: access the maximum at the root; insert and extract-max take O(log n).
A sorted array: finding the insertion point takes O(log n) comparisons, but shifting to insert takes O(n).
An unsorted array: insert takes O(1), and extracting the maximum takes O(n).
A FIFO queue: priority order follows arrival order without any extra assumptions.
hint: The structure keeps just enough order to expose the extreme quickly.
explanation: A binary max-heap keeps the maximum at its root, supports insertion and extract-max in O(log n), and exposes the max in O(1). It is not a fully sorted sequence.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 04: Heaps and Heap Sort

title: The tree planted in sorted order
prompt: An ordinary binary-search tree receives keys in ascending order. What can happen?
options: Its expected height is logarithmic for every insertion order because keys are unique.
Ascending insertion can place every key on one right-child chain, making search O(n).
It becomes a heap, so search by key takes O(log n).
Search is logarithmic even if the tree is a chain, since each comparison chooses a branch.
hint: Where does each new, larger key go?
explanation: Each new key can become the right child of the previous key, producing a path of height n. Balanced variants such as AVL trees maintain logarithmic height through rotations.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 05: Binary Search Trees

title: Rotating the tree
prompt: A self-balancing search tree becomes slightly too heavy on one side after insertion. What is the purpose of a local rotation?
options: Rotate nearby links to repair the balance condition while preserving in-order key order.
Re-sort the keys in each affected subtree, then rebuild the tree.
Swap the root with the median key; one such swap balances any tree.
Rotate any child once; every rotation reduces the tree height.
hint: The contents are ordered already; only the shape needs repair.
explanation: Rotations change local parent-child links while preserving in-order key order. AVL trees use them after updates to keep height logarithmic.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 06: AVL Trees

title: When IDs live in a small range
prompt: You need to sort 2 million integer counts, each between 0 and 999. Which method has the strongest expected advantage over comparison sorting?
options: Comparison-sort all records in O(n log n), independent of the small key range.
Counting-sort in Θ(n+k) time because k=1000 is much smaller than n.
Use a balanced tree to sort only distinct values; this is always faster than counting.
Use radix sort with one digit per record, which needs Θ(nk) work.
hint: The key range is far smaller than the number of records.
explanation: Counting sort takes O(n + k) time for n items and value range k. Here k = 1000, so it can be near-linear. It relies on the bounded integer domain; it is not a general comparison sort.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 07: Counting Sort, Radix Sort, and Lower Bounds

title: Sorting without comparing
prompt: Someone claims to comparison-sort arbitrary distinct values in worst-case O(n) time by a clever implementation. What is the best response?
options: Worst-case O(n) comparisons are possible if the input is already nearly sorted.
The comparison decision tree has to distinguish n! input orders, requiring Ω(n log n) worst-case comparisons.
Expected linear comparisons suffice for random permutations, even when every algorithm uses comparisons only.
Only recursive comparison sorts need Ω(n log n); iterative ones avoid the lower bound.
hint: How many different input orders must the comparisons distinguish?
explanation: A comparison decision tree must have at least n! leaves, one for each possible ordering of distinct inputs. A binary tree with n! leaves needs depth at least log₂(n!) = Ω(n log n), so some input requires that many comparisons.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 07: Counting Sort, Radix Sort, and Lower Bounds

title: The doubling table
prompt: A dynamic array doubles its capacity whenever full. Across many appends, why is the average copying work per append still constant?
options: There are O(log n) expansions, so the total copying across n appends is O(log n).
The largest expansion copies O(n) entries, so amortized append is also O(n).
The copied amounts form a geometric sum bounded by O(n), giving O(1) amortized copying per append.
Each insertion is O(1) worst-case because doubling leaves spare capacity.
hint: Add the copy counts at capacities 1, 2, 4, 8, ...
explanation: The total number of items copied over n appends is bounded by a geometric sum smaller than about 2n. Individual expansions cost O(n), but amortized append cost is O(1).

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 09: Table Doubling and Karp-Rabin

title: The unlucky hash table
prompt: A hash table with chaining has a good hash function on ordinary data. An adversary supplies keys that all hash to the same bucket. What is the worst-case lookup time?
options: O(1) expected if the hash assumptions and load factor hold; O(n) worst case if all keys collide.
O(log n) worst-case because a bucket chain stays balanced as it grows.
O(1) worst-case because computing the hash directly identifies the key.
O(n) expected for every load factor, but never worse than that.
hint: With every key in one chain, how long can a search through that chain take?
explanation: Expected constant time depends on assumptions about hash behavior and load. In the worst case, every key collides and a chained lookup scans O(n) entries.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 08: Hashing with Chaining

title: The typo detector
prompt: An exact document-matching tool hashes text windows to find candidates. It must never accept a false match. What must it do after a hash match?
options: Accept equality on one strong digest match; practical collision risk is negligible.
Compare the underlying windows; distinct strings can have the same finite hash.
Compare lengths only after a hash match; equal lengths imply equal contents.
Use a second independent digest; two matching finite digests prove exact equality.
hint: A finite hash maps many possible strings into fewer values.
explanation: A hash match is a candidate match, not proof of equality. Rolling hashes can make candidate discovery fast, but a direct comparison resolves collisions and protects correctness.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 09: Table Doubling and Karp-Rabin

title: The absent key
prompt: An open-addressed hash table uses linear probing. A searched key reaches an empty slot. Under standard deletion rules, when may the search stop?
options: Stop at a never-used slot; continue past a deleted marker, since a later key may share that probe sequence.
Stop at either a never-used slot or a deleted marker, since neither contains the key.
Continue through the entire table on every miss, even after a never-used slot.
Stop only after the original key's insertion position, even if the table has wrapped around.
hint: An item inserted later in the probe sequence might sit after a deleted slot.
explanation: A never-used empty slot terminates the search because insertion would have stopped there. A deleted slot must be marked separately, since a key later in that probe sequence may still be present.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 10: Open Addressing and Cryptographic Hashing

title: The unreadable file
prompt: You must compare two huge documents that often differ near the beginning. Which strategy can quickly find a mismatch without reading every character?
options: Compare whole-document hashes; they identify the location of the first difference.
Compare equal-size chunks in order and stop when one differs; an early mismatch avoids reading later chunks.
Compare every character in parallel; this reduces total input bytes read.
Sample a random offset; one unequal sample proves where the documents first differ.
hint: The first mismatch itself is a certificate that the documents differ.
explanation: A full digest can flag unequal documents but does not reveal where they differ and still reads all bytes. Ordered chunk comparison can stop early when differences appear near the start.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 02: Models of Computation, Python Cost Model, and Document Distance

title: The fewest-turn cube
prompt: A 2×2 cube puzzle is represented as a graph, with every legal turn costing one. What is the simplest search that guarantees a fewest-turn solution without maintaining priorities?
options: Breadth-first search; its layers are states at 0, 1, 2, ... turns.
Depth-first search; the first solved state has the shortest route if the graph is undirected.
Dijkstra's algorithm; unlike BFS, it works even when every edge has the same cost.
Topological sort; the puzzle states form a DAG because moves advance time.
hint: Its frontier contains one distance layer at a time.
explanation: Each edge represents one move, so all edges have equal cost. Breadth-first search explores the state graph level by level and first reaches a solved state with the minimum number of turns.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 13: Breadth-First Search

title: A negative shortcut in a DAG
prompt: A directed acyclic network has edges S→A (2), S→B (5), B→A (−10), A→T (2), and B→T (20). Which method finds the shortest weighted path from S to T efficiently?
options: Dijkstra; nonnegative edges are not needed if the graph has no cycles.
Relax edges in topological order; the best route costs −3.
Breadth-first search; the best route uses the fewest edges.
Bellman-Ford is required because no DAG-specific method supports negative weights.
hint: The negative edge is allowed in a DAG; process vertices in dependency order.
explanation: The best route is S→B→A→T with cost −3. Dijkstra may settle A at 2 and T at 4 before discovering the negative shortcut. A topological-order shortest-path pass handles negative edges in O(V+E) because the graph is acyclic.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 16: Dijkstra

title: Adding a toll to every edge
prompt: Route A has one edge of cost 5. Route B has three edges with total cost 4. If you add 1 to every edge, which route becomes shortest? What if instead you multiply every edge by 2?
options: B stays shortest under both changes because every edge changes equally.
A becomes shortest after adding 1 per edge; B stays shortest after multiplying all weights by 2.
A becomes shortest after both changes because it uses fewer edges.
Adding 1 preserves the ordering, while multiplying by 2 can reverse it.
hint: An additive toll is paid once per edge; a positive scale factor is applied to both complete path totals.
explanation: Initially B costs 4 and A costs 5. Adding 1 per edge gives A cost 6 and B cost 7, so A becomes shortest. Multiplying all edge weights by 2 preserves the original ordering, so B stays shortest.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 15: Single-Source Shortest Paths

title: One new dependency too many
prompt: A pipeline has dependencies A before B and B before C. Someone adds C before A. Can a topological ordering still schedule the three tasks?
options: Yes; start DFS at the task with no prerequisites.
No; the added edge creates a directed cycle.
Yes; reverse the order returned by a BFS.
Only if A and C run in parallel.
hint: Follow the precedence arrows from A back to A.
explanation: The three constraints now form A→B→C→A. A linear order cannot put each task before its successor all the way around the cycle.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 14: Depth-First Search and Topological Sorting

title: The edge list or the matrix?
prompt: A huge network has millions of vertices but each has only about three neighbors. Which representation is usually space-efficient?
options: An adjacency matrix; it stores O(V²) entries but offers constant-time edge checks.
An adjacency list; it uses O(V+E) storage and records only actual neighbors.
A table of all-pairs distances; it uses less space when the input graph is sparse.
A list of all vertex pairs; it stores O(V²) possible edges explicitly.
hint: Compare how many actual edges there are with the square of the number of vertices.
explanation: An adjacency list uses O(V + E) space. A matrix uses O(V²), wasteful for a sparse graph where E is only a few times V.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 13: Breadth-First Search

title: An alignment with no substitutions
prompt: Two sequences are X = ABCBDAB and Y = BDCABA. If insertions and deletions each cost 1 and substitutions are forbidden, what is the minimum edit cost?
options: 5 edits: three deletions and two insertions.
6 edits: one for each character in the shorter sequence.
7 edits: replace the entire source, since substitutions are forbidden.
4 edits: the length of the longest common subsequence.
hint: Find a longest common subsequence, then remove the other symbols and insert the symbols unique to the target.
explanation: A longest common subsequence has length 4, for example BDAB. The cost is (7−4) deletions plus (6−4) insertions, totaling 5. This uses the edit-distance/LCS relation from the course.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 21: Edit Distance, Longest Common Subsequence, Parenthesization, and Knapsack

title: The greedy alignment trap
prompt: An aligner processes X = ABCBDAB from left to right and matches each symbol to its earliest possible occurrence in Y = BDCABA, never reconsidering a match. What should you conclude?
options: The greedy match gives ABA of length 3, while BDAB is a common subsequence of length 4.
The greedy choice is optimal because the first matched symbol is always safe.
The longest common subsequence has length 6 because Y has six symbols.
No common subsequence exists because the first symbols differ.
hint: The first A in X occurs late in Y, even though B and D at the start of Y can form a longer shared subsequence.
explanation: Greedy first matches the A in X to the A at position 4 of Y. Continuing gives ABA, length 3. But BDAB is a common subsequence of length 4. A local earliest match can block the globally longest alignment.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 21: Edit Distance, Longest Common Subsequence, Parenthesization, and Knapsack

title: The density-first trap
prompt: A 0/1 knapsack holds weight 50. Whole items have (value, weight): A=(60,10), B=(100,20), and C=(120,30). A greedy rule takes the highest value-per-weight first. What happens?
options: The density-first rule takes A then B for 160; B+C is feasible and yields 220.
The density-first rule takes B then C for 220, which is the optimal subset.
The density-first rule takes A+C for 180 because A has the top density.
The density-first rule takes A+B for 160 and is optimal because A has the highest value.
hint: The top-density choice leaves too little capacity for the most valuable pair.
explanation: A has the highest density, so greedy takes A and then B, for total weight 30 and value 160. The feasible pair B+C fills the capacity and gives value 220. Density-first is optimal for fractional knapsack, but it can fail when each item must be taken whole.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 21: Edit Distance, Longest Common Subsequence, Parenthesization, and Knapsack

title: The missing state in a DP cache
prompt: A knapsack solver caches the best value using only the next-item index i as its key. The same suffix is reached with remaining capacities 3 and 8. What is wrong?
options: The key must include both i and remaining capacity; those calls are different subproblems.
The key should be only remaining capacity, since item order does not affect feasibility.
The cache is valid if all item values are positive.
The cache is valid, but the answer must be recomputed after each recursive return.
hint: Can the best choice among the remaining items be identical for both capacities?
explanation: The suffix alone does not determine the subproblem answer. Its remaining capacity matters too, so the cache state must include both i and capacity. Otherwise one call can reuse an answer computed for a different budget.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 21: Edit Distance, Longest Common Subsequence, Parenthesization, and Knapsack

title: Choose the matrix-chain split
prompt: Multiply A (10×100), B (100×5), and C (5×50). Which parenthesization uses fewer scalar multiplications?
options: (AB)C, about 7,500 operations; A(BC) costs about 75,000.
A(BC), about 7,500 operations; (AB)C costs about 75,000.
Both cost the same because matrix multiplication is associative.
(AB)C, about 750 operations; A(BC) costs about 7,500.
hint: For each multiplication, multiply rows of the left matrix by columns of the right matrix and by the shared dimension.
explanation: (AB)C costs 10·100·5 + 10·5·50 = 7,500. A(BC) costs 100·5·50 + 10·100·50 = 75,000. The product is the same, but intermediate shapes change the work by a factor of ten.
