source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 21: Edit Distance, Longest Common Subsequence, Parenthesization, and Knapsack

title: A million-step robot
prompt: A robot's shortest path on a grid can use only local moves. Why might a graph search still be impractical when the map has a million cells?
options: BFS runs in O(V+E), but may still visit Θ(V+E) reachable states and consume substantial memory.
BFS runs in O(log V) on sparse graphs because the frontier grows one layer at a time.
BFS explores every possible route, so its work is exponential in the number of paths.
BFS needs a dense graph; with local edges it cannot reach distant grid cells.
hint: A linear-time method can still be large when the input itself is huge.
explanation: BFS is O(V + E), which is optimal up to reading the graph but can still touch millions of vertices. Big-O compares growth; it does not guarantee a small absolute runtime.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 13: Breadth-First Search

title: One Newton step
prompt: For f(x)=x²−2, Newton's update from x₀=1 is x₁ = x₀−f(x₀)/f′(x₀). What is x₁?
hint: At x=1, f(x)=−1 and f′(x)=2.
explanation: Substitute x₀=1: x₁=1−(−1)/2=1.5. Newton's method uses the local tangent; later steps converge quickly to √2.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 12: Square Roots and Newton's Method

title: Karatsuba's surprise
prompt: Multiplying two n-digit numbers by splitting each into high and low halves usually creates four half-size products. Karatsuba uses one fewer product. Why does this matter?
options: Three half-size multiplications change the recurrence to about 3T(n/2)+O(n), improving its exponent.
Three multiplications halve the number of recursion levels, making the algorithm O(log n).
The trick removes all additions, so the remaining work is O(n).
It improves only a constant factor because recursive products are still squared in number.
hint: The number of recursive subproducts drives the asymptotic recurrence.
explanation: Karatsuba computes the cross term from a third product plus additions and subtractions. Three half-size multiplications give roughly O(n^log₂3), better asymptotically than O(n²).

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 11: Integer Arithmetic and Karatsuba Multiplication

title: Unroll the merge recurrence
prompt: A recursive method makes two calls on problems of size n/2 and spends cn work merging their results. If T(1) is constant, what is the asymptotic runtime?
options: Θ(n log n).
Θ(n).
Θ(n²).
Θ(log n).
hint: Each recursion level does about cn total merge work, and there are logarithmically many levels.
explanation: The recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+cn has Θ(n) work per level across Θ(log n) levels, so its total is Θ(n log n).

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 03: Insertion Sort and Merge Sort

title: A heap for the sparse map
prompt: Dijkstra must run on a graph with one million vertices and about three million edges. Which priority-queue choice avoids the array implementation's quadratic scan for the minimum?
options: A binary min-heap supports logarithmic extract-min and decrease-key in the standard course implementation.
An unsorted array, since both operations take O(1) time.
A sorted array, since insertion and extract-min both take O(log V) time.
A FIFO queue, because positive weights make vertices settle in insertion order.
hint: The algorithm repeatedly needs the smallest unsettled tentative distance.
explanation: A binary min-heap supports extract-min and decrease-key in logarithmic time, for O((V + E) log V) overall. An array priority queue scans all V entries to find each minimum, costing O(V² + E), which is poor on a sparse graph.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 16: Dijkstra

title: Count every shortest route
prompt: In a unit-edge graph, S connects to A and C; both A and C connect to B. BFS discovers B from A first. When it later scans edge C→B, what should it do to count all shortest routes to B?
options: Ignore C→B because BFS has already marked B visited.
Add the number of shortest routes to C to B's count, since it reaches B at the same minimum distance.
Replace B's distance with dist(C)+1 and reset its count to one.
Run a second BFS from C, then subtract the routes already found from A.
hint: C is at the same BFS distance as A, so it offers another predecessor on a shortest route.
explanation: On first discovery, set B's distance to dist(A)+1 and initialize its path count from A. When C reaches an already discovered B with dist(C)+1 equal to dist(B), add the number of shortest routes to C. Do not discard the second equal-length predecessor.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 13: Breadth-First Search

title: A cycle that pays you to loop
prompt: A source reaches a cycle of total weight −2, and from that cycle there is a path to T. What is the shortest-walk cost from the source to T?
options: There is no finite minimum; each extra loop lowers the walk cost by 2.
The minimum uses the cycle exactly once, because shortest paths cannot repeat vertices.
There is a finite shortest walk unless every edge in the cycle is negative.
The answer is unchanged; cycles affect only routes that end on the cycle.
hint: How does the cost change if you traverse the cycle one more time before leaving for T?
explanation: Each cycle traversal subtracts another 2, and any number of traversals is possible before reaching T. The infimum is unbounded below, so there is no finite shortest-walk cost.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 17: Bellman-Ford

title: The memory-time trade
prompt: A team speeds up repeated searches by precomputing and storing all pairwise distances among n states. What is the main trade-off?
options: It answers queries quickly but needs Θ(n²) stored distances; an edge change can invalidate many entries.
It needs Θ(E) extra storage and stays valid after any edge-weight change.
It reduces preprocessing to O(n) because each vertex stores one predecessor.
It answers queries in O(log V) while using less space than the original graph.
hint: How many ordered pairs of states are there?
explanation: All-pairs results require O(n²) entries. They can make queries fast, but the memory and preprocessing cost grow quadratically and updates may invalidate the table.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 15: Single-Source Shortest Paths

title: The fast search that copies too much
prompt: A Python binary search recurses on A[:mid] or A[mid+1:]. Comparisons inspect only O(log n) midpoints. What is its total running-time order?
options: O(log n), under the common model where list slicing is constant time.
O(n), because copied slice lengths form a geometric sum.
O(n log n), because each level copies n elements.
O(n²), because all previous slices are copied again.
hint: At successive calls, copied slices have sizes near n/2, n/4, n/8, and so on.
explanation: The recursive slices copy about n/2 + n/4 + n/8 + ... = O(n) elements in total. Comparisons take O(log n), so slicing removes the logarithmic-time advantage; use index bounds into the original list instead.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 02: Models of Computation, Python Cost Model, and Document Distance

title: A window that slides
prompt: A text-matching algorithm hashes each fixed-length substring. After moving the window by one character, how can a rolling hash help?
options: Remove the outgoing symbol's weighted contribution, shift the remaining hash, and add the incoming symbol.
Recompute all m symbols per window; rolling hashes reduce the number of windows instead.
A matching rolling hash proves exact equality because adjacent windows overlap.
Hash only every mth window, then interpolate the unexamined positions.
hint: Adjacent windows share all but two characters.
explanation: A rolling hash reuses the previous window's value, updating it in constant time for a suitable polynomial hash. Any hash match still needs verification to guard against collisions.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 09: Table Doubling and Karp-Rabin

title: Polynomial, with an asterisk
prompt: A knapsack algorithm runs in O(nS), where S is an integer capacity written in binary. A student says this is polynomial-time because the expression is polynomial in S. What is the catch?
options: O(nS) is polynomial in the numeric S, but S can be exponential in its binary encoding length; this is pseudo-polynomial.
It is polynomial in input length because binary S takes log S bits.
It is strongly polynomial because dynamic programs are independent of numeric values.
It is exponential even when S is given in unary.
hint: Compare S with the length of its binary representation.
explanation: If S is encoded with log₂S bits, then an O(nS) runtime can be exponential in the input length. It is polynomial in the numeric capacity, so it is called pseudo-polynomial, not generally a polynomial-time algorithm.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.006, Lecture 21: Edit Distance, Longest Common Subsequence, Parenthesization, and Knapsack

title: The duplicated patient
prompt: You split a clinical table row-by-row at random. Each patient contributes ten rows, and the model scores 99% on held-out rows. What is the main concern?
options: The split lets patient-specific measurements appear in both sets
Removing the patient ID guarantees the split tests new patients
Ten visits per patient provide ten independent examples
A large row-level test set eliminates within-patient dependence
hint: What is the unit that must be new at deployment?
explanation: Rows from one patient share stable signals. A row split can put those signals in training and test, so it estimates performance on new rows from familiar patients rather than new patients.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: Uncertainty has blind spots
prompt: A label budget is spent mostly on borderline compounds from one large scaffold family. You need a model that transfers to new scaffold families. What change best addresses the gap?
options: Add scaffold diversity to acquisition and keep scaffold-held-out evaluation
Intensify uncertainty sampling within the same scaffold family
Choose compounds by training error and evaluate on those acquired labels
Keep a random row split and increase the number of examples from the dominant scaffold
hint: Boundary uncertainty and coverage of the future population are different goals.
explanation: An uncertainty-only sampler can over-focus on a dense region. Diverse acquisition can cover other structures; evaluation should still hold out scaffolds to measure transfer.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 5: Active Learning

title: A batch effect with perfect timing
prompt: Every positive sample was run in batch A, and every negative in batch B. A classifier is perfect on a random split. Which follow-up best tests whether it learned biology rather than batch?
options: Collect blinded samples with both labels represented in each batch
Add batch ID as a covariate and keep the same random split
Repeat the random split of the same confounded data
Choose the model with the sparsest feature attribution on the existing data
hint: The original design has no observations that separate label from batch.
explanation: A random split preserves the confound. A crossed, blinded collection creates examples that can distinguish biological signal from batch effects.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: Two moons, one centroid
prompt: Two crescent-shaped clusters curve around each other. K-means cuts across the middle. Which change better matches the geometry?
options: Use a graph-based clustering objective based on neighborhood connectivity
Run the same two-centroid k-means objective for more iterations
Increase restarts while retaining the same centroid objective
Replace the Euclidean distance by its square without changing the objective
hint: The issue is the shape assumed by the clustering objective, not an unlucky initialization.
explanation: K-means favors compact centroid-based groups. A graph method can use neighborhood connectivity to separate non-convex shapes.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 18: Spectral Clustering

title: The held-out hospital
prompt: You want to estimate performance at hospitals absent from training. Which validation design matches that target?
options: Hold out complete hospitals and evaluate on them
Hold out visits at random within each known hospital
Hold out patients while keeping every hospital in training
Tune on the new hospitals and report the score used for tuning
hint: Match the split unit to the deployment change.
explanation: Holding out sites tests transfer to unseen hospitals. Random visit splits mostly test new samples from familiar sites.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: Same score, different confidence
prompt: Two classifiers have the same accuracy at threshold 0.5. For B's cases assigned probability 0.99, only 80% are positive. What property does accuracy fail to distinguish?
options: Calibration
Sensitivity at the 0.5 threshold
Ordering of positive and negative examples
The positive class frequency in the whole dataset
hint: Compare assigned probabilities with observed frequencies within a score group.
explanation: A calibrated group assigned probability 0.99 should be positive about 99% of the time. This group is overconfident despite the same accuracy.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 4: Regularization and Logistic Regression

title: When is a follow-up worth it?
prompt: A calibrated model estimates 10% disease risk. Missing a case costs 20 units; a definitive follow-up test costs 1 and prevents that missed-case loss, with no other costs. Is follow-up worthwhile?
options: Yes; expected no-test cost is 2, above the test cost of 1
No; 10% is below the conventional 50% threshold
No; the missed-case cost should be divided by the disease probability
Test only when the cost is below the probability itself
hint: Compare p times the missed-case cost with the test cost.
explanation: Without testing, expected cost is 0.1 times 20 = 2. Testing costs 1, so it has lower expected cost under these assumptions. The implied threshold is 0.05, not 0.5.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 4: Regularization and Logistic Regression

title: A regularizer with a job
prompt: A high-dimensional linear model has low training error and coefficients that vary sharply across nearby training samples. What is a sensible next step?
options: Increase regularization, then compare stability and held-out error
Decrease regularization so the coefficients fit each sample more exactly
Select features using repeated final-test evaluations
Add more highly correlated features before examining validation performance
hint: The concern is sensitivity to the sample, not lack of optimization time.
explanation: Stronger regularization can reduce coefficient variance at the cost of fit. Held-out evaluation measures whether the tradeoff helps generalization.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 4: Regularization and Logistic Regression

title: Two copies of the same feature
prompt: Two columns are exact copies in a ridge design matrix. For a fixed prediction, their coefficients must sum to c. Which split minimizes β1² + β2²?
options: β1 = c/2 and β2 = c/2
Put all c on one copy and zero on the other
Any split has the same squared penalty
The split depends on which copy was inserted first
hint: Minimize the sum of squares while holding the sum fixed.
explanation: The squared coefficients have the smallest sum when equal. Ridge spreads weight across duplicate columns, so individual coefficients are not uniquely interpretable without the penalty.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 4: Regularization and Logistic Regression

title: Rescale the feature, change the penalty
prompt: You replace x by 10x and its coefficient β by β/10, preserving every prediction. Under the same L2 penalty, what happens to this coefficient's penalty?
options: It falls to one hundredth of its former value
It stays fixed because predictions did not change
It decreases tenfold, rather than one hundredfold
It increases one hundredfold because the feature is larger
hint: Compare β² with (β/10)².
explanation: The squared coefficient shrinks by a factor of 100. A fixed ridge penalty depends on feature units, so standardization or scale-aware penalties matter.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 4: Regularization and Logistic Regression

title: Which lambda wins?
prompt: Training loss falls as ridge λ gets smaller, but cross-validation loss has a minimum at a moderate λ. Which choice best targets future performance?
options: Select the moderate λ with the lowest cross-validation loss
Select the smallest lambda because it minimizes training loss
Select the largest lambda because simpler models always transfer best
Choose lambda after comparing scores on the final test set
hint: Training and validation loss answer different questions.
explanation: Choose the hyperparameter using validation data that approximates the target use. The smallest penalty can overfit; the largest can underfit.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 4: Regularization and Logistic Regression

title: The batch is the label
prompt: Every positive microscopy image contains a blue calibration bar; negatives do not. The bar will be absent after deployment. What is the main risk?
options: The model may use the bar as a shortcut that fails after the pipeline changes
The bar makes the cell-type signal identifiable despite the confounding
A random split rules out reliance on the bar
More training examples from the same pipeline guarantee the bar will be ignored
hint: Ask whether the cue comes from the target or the collection process.
explanation: The bar predicts the label in this dataset but is not stable at deployment. Good in-distribution accuracy does not establish that the model learned the biological signal.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: The test set has a job
prompt: You use 8,000 examples for fitting, 1,000 for choosing models and thresholds, and 1,000 once for a final estimate. Which set should choose the threshold?
options: The validation set
The final test set, because it is reserved for future-performance estimates
The training set alone, because the threshold is a model parameter
A pooled validation and test set, followed by reporting the same pooled score
hint: Threshold tuning is a model-selection decision.
explanation: Use validation data for selection. Reusing the final test set makes its later estimate optimistic.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: Hard examples are not always bad examples
prompt: Boosting keeps increasing attention on misclassified examples. Many are later found to have incorrect microscopy labels. What is a likely risk?
options: It can focus later learners on annotation noise and hurt performance on clean data
Later learners can infer the intended labels from high example weights
Incorrect labels stop affecting the ensemble after their weights get large
A low final training error rules out sensitivity to annotation noise
hint: The algorithm observes an error, but not why it occurred.
explanation: Boosting emphasizes hard cases. If many are mislabeled, it can spend capacity on annotation noise and lose performance on clean future samples.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 12: Combining Classifiers and Boosting

title: Time remembers what a mixture forgets
prompt: A sensor alternates between two physical modes. A Gaussian mixture gives implausible probability to rapid switches. What does a Markov state model add?
options: Transition probabilities that link latent modes across adjacent times
A constraint that makes all observation noise disappear
A requirement that both latent modes occur equally often
An independence assumption between states at neighboring time steps
hint: A static mixture chooses a component independently at each observation.
explanation: A hidden Markov model links latent states with transition probabilities, so it can represent persistence and reduce probability on implausible switches.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 19: Hidden Markov Models

title: The loss chooses the answer
prompt: For labels 1, 2, and 9, which constant prediction minimizes squared loss and which minimizes absolute loss?
options: Squared loss is minimized at 4; absolute loss at 2
Both losses are minimized at 4
Both losses are minimized at 2
Squared loss is minimized at 2; absolute loss at 4
hint: For squared error use the mean; for absolute error use a median.
explanation: Squared loss is minimized by the mean, (1+2+9)/3 = 4. Absolute loss is minimized by a median, here 2. The loss function changes the optimal constant prediction.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.390: Regression Lab

title: A change of coordinates for logistic regression
prompt: Unregularized logistic regression includes an intercept and uses all columns of x. Replace x by z = Ax for invertible square A, then optimize the same likelihood globally. What happens to fitted probabilities on these examples?
options: They can remain exactly the same after reparameterizing coefficients
Probabilities must change whenever the feature axes change
Only binary decisions, not probabilities, can be preserved
Probabilities are preserved only when A is orthogonal
hint: An invertible coordinate change preserves the set of linear scores.
explanation: The coefficients can be mapped through A to recover the same linear score and probabilities. Regularization can break this invariance because its norm depends on coordinates.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 4: Regularization and Logistic Regression

title: An RBF SVM far from home
prompt: For an RBF-kernel SVM with nonzero intercept, a test point moves far from every training example. What does its score approach?
options: The intercept, as kernel contributions tend to zero
The nearest support vector's label, regardless of distance
Zero, regardless of the fitted intercept
The sum of all support-vector coefficients, because distant kernels tend to one
hint: RBF similarity decays with squared distance.
explanation: Each training-point similarity tends to zero far from the data, leaving the intercept. Its sign depends on that fitted intercept; distance alone does not imply a negative prediction.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 8: Support Vector Machines and Kernels

title: Margin, please
prompt: Two hard-margin separators classify the training set correctly. One has a wider geometric margin. Why might the maximum-margin rule prefer it?
options: It can tolerate larger small perturbations before a point crosses the boundary
It must have higher training accuracy even when both classify every point correctly
It guarantees lower error under any distribution shift
It gives the same answer under arbitrary feature rescaling
hint: Consider how far a training point can move before crossing the boundary.
explanation: The geometric margin is a buffer to the nearest training points. It can improve robustness to small perturbations, though it cannot guarantee performance under arbitrary shifts.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 3: Support Vector Machine

title: Can two classifiers help each other?
prompt: Two binary classifiers make mistakes on exactly the same 20 validation examples and are correct on the same remaining examples. With a fixed tie-break rule, can their majority vote reduce 0-1 error?
options: No lower 0-1 error than either classifier
Voting lowers error if the two confidence scores differ
Voting lowers error whenever each model beats random guessing
Calibration alone makes hard majority voting correct some shared mistakes
hint: For binary labels, if both agree on which examples are right and wrong, compare their hard predictions.
explanation: On every example both predict the true label or both predict the other label, so their hard predictions coincide. Voting cannot reduce their error; useful ensembles need diversity in their mistakes.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 12: Combining Classifiers and Boosting

title: When the reward lies
prompt: A robot earns reward for reaching a delivery zone. It finds a nearby loop that triggers the reward repeatedly without delivering. What failed?
options: The reward made a proxy behavior more valuable than delivery
The agent failed to optimize the reward it actually received
The main problem is that the transition dynamics are not deterministic
A larger training set necessarily aligns the proxy with the intended task
hint: The agent optimized the specified score successfully.
explanation: An agent maximizes its reward, not an unstated goal. A proxy reward can invite behavior that raises the score while missing the intended outcome.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.390 Reinforcement Learning Lab

title: Learn the map or learn by trying
prompt: In a small grid, transition probabilities are known exactly in version A and unknown but observed through experience in version B. Which method pairing fits?
options: Value iteration for A; Q-learning from samples for B
Value iteration from the unknown model in B; Q-learning only in A
Value iteration in both, since a single reward observation specifies all transitions
Neither method can use observations of the next state
hint: One method plans from a supplied model; the other learns values from experience.
explanation: Value iteration uses the transition and reward model. Q-learning updates action values from observed state, action, reward, and next-state samples without requiring transition probabilities in advance.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.390 Reinforcement Learning Lab

title: The feature scale trap
prompt: A perceptron uses molecular weight near 50,000 and a binary motif flag. Updates are unstable. Which change helps conditioning without changing labels?
options: Scale from training-set statistics, then reuse that transform at evaluation
Scale training and test features separately using each set's own distribution
Leave raw units because perceptron updates are invariant to separate feature rescaling
Drop the motif flag solely because its numerical values are smaller
hint: Feature units can change the size of gradient updates.
explanation: Scaling can improve optimization. Estimate the transformation on training data and apply it unchanged to validation and test data to avoid leakage.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: A category is not a ruler
prompt: In a linear regression model with an intercept, assay platform IDs 1, 2, and 3 are encoded as one numeric feature. What assumption does this representation impose on the platform effect?
options: Platform effects follow a meaningful order with equally spaced steps
The platforms are exchangeable under any permutation of their IDs
Each platform contributes the same number of training examples
Each platform gets an independently estimated coefficient
hint: Would changing the arbitrary names alter the model's geometry?
explanation: One numeric coefficient makes the platform contribution change by the same amount from 1 to 2 as from 2 to 3. Dummy variables can represent distinct platform effects without imposing this arbitrary linear spacing.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: The missingness oracle
prompt: A feature is missing in 80% of one hospital's records and 5% of another's. A model uses missingness to predict outcome. What should you check first?
options: Whether missingness marks site or workflow and whether that persists
Whether zero imputation improves another random split of the same hospitals
Whether more trees can reconstruct every missing value
Whether a higher pooled score makes the missingness process irrelevant
hint: Missingness can reveal how data were collected.
explanation: Missingness may carry real signal, but its mechanism can vary across sites and time. Check the data process and evaluate in settings that match deployment.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: The confident wrong map
prompt: A classifier has high AUROC but poor calibration. You use it only to rank compounds for a fixed-capacity queue. What follows?
options: The ranking may still help, but probability-based choices need calibrated risks
Poor calibration necessarily makes the ranking uninformative
High AUROC guarantees excellent precision at this particular queue size
AUROC determines the calibrated probability cutoff for the queue
hint: Ranking and the numerical meaning of a probability are different properties.
explanation: AUROC measures ranking across thresholds; calibration compares probability values with observed frequencies. Ranking may help triage, while risk-based choices need meaningful probabilities.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: Same average, different people
prompt: Two models have the same overall error. One has similar error in two groups; the other is excellent in one and poor in the other. What report helps a high-stakes decision?
options: Subgroup errors with uncertainty, alongside the overall result
Report only pooled error because it fully determines errors in every group
Report subgroup rates without their sample sizes or uncertainty
Select the model with fewer coefficients without reporting group results
hint: A single average can hide who bears the errors.
explanation: Stratified results and uncertainty can reveal variation that an overall score hides. Interpretation still depends on sample sizes and the intended use.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: A step across the valley
prompt: For f(w) = w²/2, gradient descent starts at w = 1 with step size 2.2, landing at -1.2 where loss is larger. Which diagnosis fits?
options: The step is beyond the stable range for this quadratic
Convexity failed because the loss increased after an update
The analytical gradient points uphill at w = 1
A smaller step would change the location of the quadratic's minimum
hint: The gradient is w; apply w_new = w - ηw and compare losses.
explanation: The update gives -1.2, so squared loss grows. Convexity does not protect against an oversized step; for this unit-curvature quadratic, η above 2 is unstable.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 4: Regularization and Logistic Regression

title: EM's best answer may depend on its first guess
prompt: Ten random initializations of a Gaussian mixture all improve likelihood under EM, but end at different likelihoods and assignments. What is the best reading?
options: EM can reach different local optima; best likelihood does not establish semantic meaning
Monotone likelihood improvement proves a global optimum
The most evenly sized clusters must give the global optimum
Different endpoints prove at least one EM implementation is wrong
hint: Monotone objective improvement need not find the global optimum.
explanation: EM increases likelihood at each iteration but can converge to a local optimum. Multiple starts reveal sensitivity; likelihood alone does not tell whether clusters are meaningful.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 15: Mixture Models and EM

title: Covariate shift, with a catch
prompt: Training and deployment differ in p(x), while p(y|x) is assumed unchanged and deployment has training support. Which strategy is defensible?
options: Consider density-ratio weighting and check support and weight stability
Ignore the changed feature distribution because conditional labels are unchanged
Give more weight to examples that are more common in training than deployment
Tune against deployment test labels, then use that same score as the final estimate
hint: The target risk averages conditional error under a different x distribution.
explanation: Under covariate shift with support, weighting by target-to-source density ratio can align risks. Estimated ratios can be unstable, and the unchanged-conditional assumption needs checking.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 5: Active Learning

title: The point far outside the margin
prompt: A hard-margin linear SVM is fit to separable data. You add a correctly labeled point far beyond the current margin. Assume it remains outside the margin. What happens?
options: The separating hyperplane remains unchanged
The margin must grow because the sample count increased
Every added point becomes a support vector
The offset must move until the added point touches the margin
hint: Which examples constrain the maximum-margin optimum?
explanation: Points on the margin determine the hard-margin solution. A correctly labeled point beyond it adds no active constraint and leaves the optimum unchanged.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 3: Support Vector Machine

title: A monotone fix for probability scores
prompt: A strictly increasing transform changes model scores but preserves every pairwise ordering. Which property is guaranteed?
options: AUROC is unchanged, while calibration may change
Both ranking and calibration are unchanged
Calibration stays fixed while AUROC changes
Both improve whenever the transform is smooth
hint: AUROC uses pair ordering; calibration uses score values.
explanation: A strictly increasing transform preserves positive-negative rankings, so AUROC is unchanged. It changes numerical probabilities and may help or harm calibration.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 4: Regularization and Logistic Regression

title: Filtering or smoothing the hidden state?
prompt: An online sensor must estimate hidden state X_t before the next reading arrives. Which posterior uses only information available then?
options: P(X_t | readings through t)
P(X_t | readings through the final time T, with T greater than t)
P(X_t | readings through t+1)
P(X_t | the next reading only)
hint: Online inference cannot use observations that have not arrived.
explanation: Filtering uses observations through the current time. Smoothing uses the full sequence, including later observations; forward-backward inference combines past and future evidence.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 19: Hidden Markov Models

title: When labels disagree
prompt: Experts often disagree on a subtle microscopy label. A model is scored against the same annotator who labeled its training data. What can a high score fail to establish?
options: That the model captures the biological construct rather than one annotation policy
The model's observed agreement with the chosen annotator on the scored examples
The measured rate of matching that annotator's held-out labels
Performance relative to that particular annotation rule on this evaluation set
hint: The reference label is itself a measurement with uncertainty.
explanation: A model can reproduce one annotation process without resolving ambiguity or matching the biological construct. Inter-rater variation and the intended use matter.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.036 Lab 2: Features; Train / Test (Spring 2021)

title: A discount changes the preferred route
prompt: Route A gives +1 now and stops. Route B gives +3 exactly three steps later and no other reward. With γ = 0.5, which route has larger discounted return?
options: A, because 1 is greater than 3 × 0.5³
Route B, because its undiscounted reward is three times larger
They tie, since each route produces only one nonzero reward
Route B, because discounting increases later rewards
hint: Discount the delayed reward by γ³.
explanation: Route B is worth 3 × 0.5³ = 0.375, below A's 1. A larger discount factor can make the delayed reward more valuable.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.390 Reinforcement Learning Lab

title: One alarm, two suspects
prompt: Burglary and earthquake are independent rare events. In this simplified model, the alarm rings if and only if at least one occurs. After hearing the alarm, you learn an earthquake definitely occurred. Compared with knowing only about the alarm, how does the probability of burglary change?
options: It becomes less likely because the earthquake now explains the alarm
Burglary becomes more likely because the two causes were initially independent
Burglary becomes impossible once an earthquake is confirmed
Burglary stays at its alarm-only posterior because the report did not mention burglary
hint: Evidence for one cause can reduce the need for another cause of the same effect.
explanation: The earthquake alone fully accounts for the alarm in this model. Once it is confirmed, burglary returns to its prior probability because the causes were independent. That is lower than its alarm-only posterior: observing a common effect can make otherwise independent causes dependent.

source.title: MIT OCW 6.867 Lecture 21: Bayesian Networks

title: The Unreadable Decree
prompt: A ruler posts a rule where no one can read it, then punishes a shopkeeper for breaking it. Which rule-of-law concern is most directly raised?
options: Whether the ruler's private aim should override the wording people could read
Whether people had fair notice of the rule that now governs their conduct
Whether the rule limits the shopkeeper's freedom for the shopkeeper's own welfare
Whether the posted notice supplies evidence that the rule caused a loss
hint: Think about how a law's meaning becomes available to the people it governs.
explanation: A publicity concern asks whether people can discover the announced law. Secret intentions cannot fairly supply the public standard. This is a thought experiment about interpretation, not a claim about any current legal system.

source.title: Session 6: Scalia and Dworkin on Statutory Interpretation, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Rulebook Behind the Rulebook
prompt: A town accepts a specific test for deciding whether a proposed rule is legally valid: it must pass a stated council vote and receive the mayor's signature. In Hart's vocabulary, what kind of rule supplies that test?
options: A primary rule that directly requires residents to behave in a certain way
A rule of recognition that identifies valid rules by their source or form
A rule of adjudication that tells officials how to settle disputes about a rule
A rule of change that gives an official power to introduce or repeal rules
hint: One rule governs conduct; the other governs the creation of rules.
explanation: Hart distinguishes primary rules, which guide or restrict conduct, from secondary rules that identify, change, or adjudicate primary rules. A procedure for valid enactment is a secondary rule, often discussed as a rule of change or recognition.

source.title: Session 3: Hart, selections from The Concept of Law, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Tiny Fine
prompt: Mira stops at red lights only because she expects a fine. Sol stops because they treat the light as a shared standard that gives them a reason to act. Which description captures Sol's attitude in Hart's framework?
options: An outward habit: people stop because red lights have usually been followed by other drivers
A prediction: people stop because a fine is likely if they do not
An internal point of view: the light is treated as a shared reason or standard for stopping
An official test: the light is treated as legally valid because an authority approved it
hint: Would a camera observing only behavior distinguish the two people?
explanation: The same outward behavior can be mere habit or compliance from an internal point of view. Hart's account emphasizes that participants can treat rules as standards for criticism and reasons for conduct, not just as predictions of punishment.

source.title: Session 3: Hart, selections from The Concept of Law, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Why Punish? Two Questions
prompt: A city debates why it should maintain a system of punishment and why a particular person should be punished under it. Which distinction best captures Rawls's proposal?
options: Use likely social benefits to justify the institution, while judging an individual case under the practice's rules and standards of desert
Use likely social benefits to justify both the institution and each verdict, recalculating welfare for every defendant
Use desert to justify the institution, but deterrence alone to decide which individual receives punishment
Treat institutional design and individual verdicts as the same question because both involve state action
hint: Separate the reason for adopting a practice from the reason for applying its rules to a person.
explanation: Rawls suggests that forward-looking utility can justify adopting a practice of punishment, while individual decisions within that practice can be governed by retributive rules. This avoids asking a judge to punish an innocent person simply because doing so might produce good consequences. The distinction is a proposal, not an uncontested account of punishment.

source.title: Session 18: Rawls, Two Concepts of Rules, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: A Law Can Be Unjust
prompt: A rule was adopted through the system's accepted process, but it treats a minority unfairly. Which claim best fits legal positivism as presented in the course notes?
options: A rule can be legally valid under accepted social criteria and still be morally unjust
A rule becomes legally valid only when its content meets an independent moral standard
A rule is legally valid only if most residents obey it in ordinary cases
A rule has legal status only after a court endorses its moral justification
hint: The position separates social facts about legal status from moral appraisal.
explanation: The Hart session presents positivism as separating what the law is from what it ought to be. This lets someone identify a rule as legally valid under social criteria while still criticizing it as unjust. The ethical evaluation remains open.

source.title: Session 3: Hart, selections from The Concept of Law, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The New Referee
prompt: A town's accepted rulebook says a new waste rule is valid after three of five council members vote for it. A newcomer takes the council seat, and the town continues using that procedure. Why does this case trouble a simple 'law is whatever the ruler commands' theory?
options: The new leader's commands become law through a fresh habit of obedience to that person
The office and its accepted rules can persist when its occupant changes
Every earlier law must be explicitly reissued by the incoming leader
A majority's current preference alone determines which old rules remain binding
hint: What persists when the office-holder changes?
explanation: Hart's notes discuss continuity across changes of sovereign and ask what makes an office distinct from its occupant. Accepted secondary rules can explain why the same institutional role and valid procedures persist through personnel changes, without treating every utterance by a ruler as law.

source.title: Session 3: Hart, selections from The Concept of Law, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Who gets to change the rule?
prompt: A town gives its elected council the power to introduce, amend, or repeal traffic duties through a majority vote. In Hart's framework, what kind of rule gives the council this power?
options: A primary rule setting a traffic duty
A rule of adjudication authorizing courts to settle disputes
A rule of recognition supplying criteria for valid law
A rule of change enabling officials to alter rules
hint: Distinguish identifying a valid rule from having the institutional power to change it.
explanation: Hart distinguishes rules of change from rules of recognition and adjudication. A rule of change confers the power to introduce, alter, or remove rules; recognition concerns criteria of validity, and adjudication concerns deciding disputes.

source.title: Session 3: Hart, selections from The Concept of Law, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Contract Recipe
prompt: A law tells people which signatures make a contract legally effective. The law does not order anyone to sign. Why is this a problem for a theory that treats every law as a threat-backed command?
options: It imposes a duty to sign a contract and backs that duty with a penalty
It confers a legal power that a person may use by following the required steps
It predicts how a judge will respond when a signature is challenged
It establishes a penalty for people who choose not to make contracts
hint: What happens if someone chooses not to use the legal procedure?
explanation: Some laws confer powers, such as how to make contracts or wills. Failing to use such a procedure need not be a violation or punishment; it can simply mean the intended legal effect does not occur. Hart uses this to challenge reducing law to duty-creating commands.

source.title: Session 3: Hart, selections from The Concept of Law, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Three Witnesses, One Principle
prompt: A fictional rule says that a valid will needs three witnesses. A judge also considers the principle that no one should profit from their own wrongdoing. In Dworkin's distinction, how do these standards differ?
options: Both are rules because each can influence a court's decision
Both are principles because each can be outweighed by other concerns
The witness requirement is a rule; the anti-wrongdoing standard is a principle with weight
The witness requirement is a policy goal; the anti-wrongdoing standard is a rule of procedure
hint: One standard has a threshold; the other can weigh alongside competing reasons.
explanation: Dworkin contrasts all-or-nothing rules with principles that have weight and may point in different directions. A principle can matter without mechanically deciding the case. The course note treats the example as an illustration of types of legal reasoning, not a universal result about wills.

source.title: Session 4: Dworkin, selections from Taking Rights Seriously, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Last Call
prompt: An umpire makes the final call in a game. What does that fact alone show about the umpire's discretion?
options: The umpire's call is final, so it cannot count as a mistake under the rules
The umpire has authority to decide, so no standards can constrain the call
The umpire needed judgment, so the game rules do not determine the result
The call may be final while still being criticizable under standards that govern the umpire
hint: Final authority and freedom from standards are different ideas.
explanation: Dworkin distinguishes discretion as judgment, as having the final say, and as being free of standards set by the authority. A decision can be final and still be criticizable as a mistake under the rules. Finality does not imply strong discretion.

source.title: Session 4: Dworkin, selections from Taking Rights Seriously, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Park's New Vehicle
prompt: A rule says, 'No vehicles in the park.' A rescue team wants to bring in a small electric cart to reach an injured visitor. The rule clearly covers cars but does not mention rescue carts. What is the philosophical issue in this example?
options: Its ordinary meaning has a clear core, but an unfamiliar case may fall near an open-textured edge
Its wording has no meaning unless a judge has already applied it to every possible case
The rule is invalid whenever its author did not list a rescue cart as an example
The cart's electric motor places it outside the rule regardless of the rule's purpose
hint: The example tests where a clear rule meets an unanticipated case.
explanation: Hart uses rules such as 'no vehicles in the park' to illustrate a penumbra of uncertain applications. A judge or official may need judgment when the core meaning does not settle a new case. Philosophers disagree about whether legal principles already guide that judgment.

source.title: Session 4: Dworkin, selections from Taking Rights Seriously, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Chain Novel Judge
prompt: A judge wants a ruling to fit prior decisions while making the law's overall story as coherent and principled as possible. Which account in the course most closely matches this idea?
options: A judge should reconstruct the enacting body's private intention, regardless of later decisions
A judge should make prior decisions cohere as the best principled account of legal practice
A judge should predict the outcome another judge would choose, without evaluating principles
A judge should apply only rules whose words settle the dispute without interpretation
hint: Think of interpreting legal practice as continuing a story written by many authors.
explanation: Dworkin compares legal interpretation to writing a chain novel: each contributor must take earlier chapters seriously while making the developing work the best coherent account possible. His interpretive approach emphasizes principles and fit, rather than treating every hard case as law-free choice.

source.title: Session 4: Dworkin, selections from Taking Rights Seriously, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Fairness or Faster Roads?
prompt: A judge weighs an individual's claim to fair treatment against a proposal that would make the city more economically efficient overall. In Dworkin's terminology, which contrast is most relevant?
options: A principle protecting a person's right versus a policy aimed at a collective goal
A primary rule requiring conduct versus a secondary rule about rule-making
A valid rule versus a rule that most people follow
A reason based on the speaker's intention versus one based on causal evidence
hint: One consideration concerns justice or fairness; the other aims at a result for the community.
explanation: The session distinguishes principles, which concern justice or fairness and protect rights, from policies that aim at collective goals such as efficiency or preventing accidents. The distinction itself can be debated, but it helps identify what kind of reason is being offered.

source.title: Session 4: Dworkin, selections from Taking Rights Seriously, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Judge Who Must Think
prompt: A statute leaves a genuine ambiguity. The judge studies precedent, weighs principles, and reaches a reasoned decision. Which conclusion follows most safely from Dworkin's account?
options: A judge's final ruling shows that no legal standard applies to the case
A judge's need to reason means the written law has no role in the decision
A judge's need for judgment does not by itself show freedom from legal standards
A judge's use of principles means the ruling must create a new rule
hint: Do not confuse needing judgment with having no standards.
explanation: Dworkin argues that discretion in the ordinary sense of exercising judgment does not establish strong discretion free of the authority's standards. He disputes that an ambiguous case is necessarily a legal vacuum. Other theories may disagree about how determinate law is.

source.title: Session 4: Dworkin, selections from Taking Rights Seriously, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The private email
prompt: A statute exempts vehicles used for emergency response. An unpublished email shows that the committee chair personally had only ambulances in mind. A fire engine claims the exemption. For a textualist, what should carry the most weight?
options: The chair's unpublished intention, even if narrower than the enacted wording
The enacted words' public meaning in context
The average private preference of the legislators
Whichever outcome gives the largest economic benefit
hint: Distinguish what was enacted from one participant's unexpressed expectations.
explanation: Textualism emphasizes the publicly available meaning of the enacted text in context, rather than replacing that text with one legislator's private expectations. Context still matters; this does not reduce interpretation to reading isolated dictionary entries.

source.title: Session 6: Scalia and Dworkin on Statutory Interpretation, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Typo or Bad Idea?
prompt: A statute contains an obvious typo, but its proposed correction would also change the policy choice the legislature made. Which correction best matches the interpretation principle discussed in the course notes?
options: Follow the printed wording literally, even when the error is unmistakable
Correct a clear slip of expression, but do not silently replace an unwise policy choice
Use the lawmaker's private intention to revise any consequence the law produces
Treat any typo as proof that the whole statute has no legal force
hint: Separate a mistake in expression from a mistake in policy.
explanation: The statutory-interpretation notes discuss correcting clear slips of the tongue or scrivener's errors while not correcting legislative mistakes of wisdom. This is presented as an interpretive position, not a rule every jurisdiction follows in every case.

source.title: Session 6: Scalia and Dworkin on Statutory Interpretation, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Original Meaning, Future Gadget
prompt: A constitution uses a phrase that once applied to telegrams. A court must decide how it relates to a new communication device. Under a textualist approach centered on original public meaning, what is the main interpretive question?
options: The private purpose each drafter hoped the clause would serve
The ordinary meaning the words have in the present day, regardless of history
The outcome most likely to protect rights under current political conditions
The text's original public meaning, read in context and applied to new cases
hint: The focus is the meaning of the enacted words, applied in context.
explanation: The notes describe textualism as focusing on objectified or semantic intent and original meaning, while acknowledging that old words can be ambiguous and must be applied to new phenomena. This still leaves interpretive disputes; it is not a mechanical lookup.

source.title: Session 6: Scalia and Dworkin on Statutory Interpretation, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Seat-Belt Puzzle
prompt: A city requires cyclists to wear helmets, saying the rule protects riders from their own injuries. Which philosophical label best fits the justification?
options: A restriction justified by preventing harm to someone other than the person restricted
Interference with a person's liberty justified by that person's own welfare
A social test for deciding which rules count as legally valid
A court's use of precedent to settle a dispute between citizens
hint: The rule limits someone's choice for that person's own welfare.
explanation: The course presents paternalism roughly as interference with liberty justified by the welfare or interests of the person whose choices are limited. Whether a particular helmet rule is justified is a further moral and empirical question.

source.title: Session 20: Gerald Dworkin's Paternalism, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Surprise Default
prompt: A benefits website silently enrolls workers in a retirement plan but lets them opt out. The employer says the default helps workers save. What makes this a useful paternalism puzzle?
options: It can steer a person's choice for their welfare even when they may opt out
It changes a person's legal rights only if the default carries a formal penalty
It proves that workers lack autonomy whenever they follow a default
It is paternalistic only if every worker receives the same financial benefit
hint: Defaults can influence behavior even when opting out remains possible.
explanation: The course notes use default options as a challenge to simple definitions of paternalism. Such a design can affect autonomy without coercive penalties. Whether it is genuinely paternalistic and whether it is justified depend on further facts and values.

source.title: Session 20: Gerald Dworkin's Paternalism, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Protecting One Group by Restricting Another
prompt: A law aims to reduce buyers' exposure to a risky product by restricting sellers' advertising. The restriction burdens sellers, while intended beneficiaries are buyers. What distinction from the course notes is relevant?
options: Pure paternalism: the restricted group and intended beneficiary group are the same
Harm prevention: the restriction is aimed only at injury sellers cause to others
Impure paternalism: one group is restricted in an effort to benefit another group
Legal adjudication: a court decides whether a buyer's choice was reasonable
hint: Compare who faces the restriction with who is supposed to benefit.
explanation: The course defines pure paternalism as restricting the same class whose welfare is promoted, and impure paternalism as restricting others in an effort to protect a class. Classification can depend on whether the law is really protecting buyers from themselves or addressing harms to others.

source.title: Session 20: Gerald Dworkin's Paternalism, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Harm Principle's Boundary
prompt: A healthy adult knowingly chooses a risky hobby that harms no one else. A proposed ban is justified only by saying, 'It is for the participant's own good.' What would Mill's harm principle put under pressure?
options: Whether preventing harm to others can justify a limit on the hobby
Whether popularity can determine which hobbies deserve legal protection
Whether risks created by public spaces should be assigned to government
Whether someone's own welfare, by itself, justifies coercion against their will
hint: The principle distinguishes preventing harm to others from compelling someone for their own benefit.
explanation: The course's discussion of Mill highlights the claim that a person's own good is not by itself enough to justify interference against their will. Applying this principle raises difficult questions about consent, risk to others, and what counts as coercion; the quiz does not declare a universal policy answer.

source.title: Session 20: Gerald Dworkin's Paternalism, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Two Bad Drivers
prompt: Two drivers behave equally recklessly. One hits a pedestrian by chance; the other does not. Why is this a classic moral-luck puzzle?
options: Only the driver whose car made contact had an intention to drive recklessly
People may judge the harmful outcome differently even when it depended on luck
A difference in outcome proves that one driver's conduct was more careful
The control principle says consequences never matter to moral assessment
hint: Hold the conduct fixed and change the outcome.
explanation: The control principle says people should not be morally assessed differently for factors beyond their control. Resultant moral luck challenges that principle because people often judge harmful outcomes more harshly than equally reckless conduct without harm. The puzzle is about our judgments, not a settled verdict.

source.title: Session 15: Cushman on causal and intentional analyses in moral judgment, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The 95% Pellet
prompt: Two people fire at a target. One fires 95 pellets, the other five. Assume both aim comparably, each pellet has the same chance to hit, and exactly one pellet hits. If no other evidence is available, what conclusion follows from the numbers alone?
options: The shooter who fired 95 pellets must have fired the target-hitting pellet; the ratio identifies the individual act.
The first shooter is more likely to have fired the target-hitting pellet, but the numbers do not identify that pellet.
The second shooter remains more likely because firing fewer pellets creates less statistical uncertainty.
Without tracing the pellet, the odds provide no reason to favor either shooter over the other.
hint: A high probability from group proportions is still different from evidence tracing this particular outcome.
explanation: Given the assumptions that each of the 100 pellets was equally likely to be the one that hit, the first shooter's pellet is overwhelmingly more likely to be responsible. But the evidence remains statistical: it does not trace the particular pellet to that shooter. The course notes use a similar two-shooter case to ask whether that probability is enough for a finding of responsibility. The sufficiency of statistical evidence is contested.

title: The Database Match
prompt: A database contains 10,000 equally plausible candidates, including one culprit. Before any testing, one candidate is selected uniformly at random. The test matches the culprit's sample 99.9% of the time and falsely matches an innocent person's sample 0.1% of the time. This selected candidate tests positive. Roughly how likely is it that this candidate is the culprit?
options: About 0.1%
About 9%
About 50%
About 99.9%
hint: Start with the selected candidate's 1-in-10,000 prior chance, then update it using the test's sensitivity and false-positive rate.
explanation: The selected candidate starts with prior probability 1/10,000. A positive test is 999 times more likely if this person is the culprit than if they are innocent (0.999 / 0.001). Updating those prior odds gives a posterior probability of about 9%. This asks about one candidate chosen before testing; it is different from selecting someone from a set of positive matches, where the expected number of false positives also matters. The session's discussion of statistical versus individualized evidence motivates why courts may ask what kind of evidence supports an individual allegation; this numerical example is an original Bayes puzzle.

source.title: Session 14: Thomson, Liability and Individualized Evidence, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Compensation Without Blame
prompt: A young child accidentally breaks a neighbor's window. The family is asked to cover the repair even though the child could not understand the risk. What does this illustrate about legal responsibility?
options: A compensation award necessarily means the person who pays deserves blame
Compensation can be assigned for reasons distinct from moral blame
A person who lacks moral blame cannot be asked to cover a loss
Legal responsibility always depends on the responsible person's intention
hint: Ask whether paying for repair must mean being blameworthy.
explanation: The causation session notes that moral responsibility can be neither necessary nor sufficient for legal responsibility. Legal systems may allocate compensation for reasons such as making losses repairable, even when moral blame is absent. Real outcomes depend on jurisdiction and facts.

source.title: Session 12: Hart and Honoré on Causation in the Law, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Company and the Employee
prompt: An employee causes damage while doing a job. A victim seeks compensation from the company, which is better able to pay, even though an executive did not personally cause the event. What issue does this raise?
options: The company can face responsibility for a work-related loss even without an executive's personal blame
The executive is liable only if they personally intended the employee's action
The employee's act automatically makes every executive morally blameworthy
Insurance can cover a loss, so the question of legal responsibility disappears
hint: Consider why a legal system might assign a loss to an organization.
explanation: Hart and Honoré's course note says legal responsibility considers factors beyond moral censure, including who is best placed to compensate. This does not settle a specific case or imply that compensation and blame are the same thing.

source.title: Session 12: Hart and Honoré on Causation in the Law, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Two Kinds of Mistake
prompt: A jury must choose a verdict under uncertainty. One kind of error convicts an innocent person; the other lets a guilty person go free. In Kaplan's decision-theoretic account, what could help explain a demanding proof standard?
options: A jury's preferred verdict should determine the threshold for each case
The strength of the evidence alone determines how costly each error is
If convicting an innocent person is treated as especially costly, the threshold can rise
Treating the errors equally always produces a higher threshold than treating them differently
hint: Decision theory compares possible outcomes and the value or cost assigned to them.
explanation: Kaplan models fact-finding as a decision under uncertainty. If convicting an innocent person is treated as especially costly relative to acquitting a guilty person, the threshold for conviction rises. This approach is debated: it depends on how costs are assigned and raises concerns about applying a case-by-case calculation to criminal verdicts.

source.title: Session 13: Kaplan, Decision Theory and the Factfinding Process, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Missing Truth
prompt: Why might a society protect open discussion even though some popular beliefs are already true?
options: Open debate can expose overlooked truth and help people understand their beliefs
Discussion is useful only when speakers already agree about the facts
Speech cannot cause harm when some part of its content is true
Truth-seeking alone settles every conflict about whether speech may be limited
hint: A true conclusion can be held without understanding its reasons.
explanation: The session presents Mill's arguments that discussion may uncover suppressed truth or parts of the truth and keep beliefs from becoming dogma. The argument relies partly on empirical claims about discussion and does not by itself settle every conflict with other values.

source.title: Session 21: Scanlon on Freedom of Expression, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Shouted Warning
prompt: A person shouts a warning to evacuate a building. It leads people to flee and also conveys the proposition that the building is unsafe. Which pairing best describes the two aspects?
options: The warning's content is locutionary; its effect on listeners is perlocutionary
The warning's content is perlocutionary; the act of warning is locutionary
The words perform an illocutionary act; their content is a rule of recognition
The words' effect is illocutionary; the sentence itself is a legal rule
hint: Separate what the words say from what they cause listeners to do.
explanation: The session on speech acts distinguishes locutionary content (the meaning of an utterance) from perlocutionary effects (what speaking brings about, such as persuading or alarming). A third category, illocutionary force, concerns what one does in speaking, such as warning or ordering.

source.title: Session 22: Langton on Speech Acts and Unspeakable Acts, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Saying It Makes It So
prompt: During a ceremony that satisfies the relevant social conventions, a person says, 'I accept.' What makes this utterance different from merely reporting, 'I accepted yesterday'?
options: The utterance can perform an act when the relevant social conditions are met
The utterance can change status only if a court records it as a legal rule
The utterance reports a past event but cannot itself alter a social relationship
The speaker's intention is sufficient to make the utterance perform the intended act
hint: Some utterances can change a social status when said under the right conditions.
explanation: The notes describe illocutionary acts such as promising, ordering, or saying 'I do' in the appropriate context. Such acts have felicity conditions: the setting, roles, and conventions matter. Intent alone may neither guarantee nor always be required for success.

source.title: Session 22: Langton on Speech Acts and Unspeakable Acts, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Accidental Order
prompt: A manager says, 'You may want to stop the machine.' The worker hears it as an order because of the manager's role and the urgent setting. What point about illocutionary acts does this test?
options: The literal wording fixes the act, whatever roles the speaker and listener occupy
The listener's response alone determines whether the utterance counts as an order
The speaker's private intention always determines the act performed
Context and authority can shape the act, even when the speaker intended advice
hint: The same sentence can function differently in different relationships and settings.
explanation: The course notes explain that the force of an utterance may depend on context and speaker position. Someone may intend advice yet successfully issue an order. Intent can matter, but it is not always necessary or sufficient for an illocutionary act.

source.title: Session 22: Langton on Speech Acts and Unspeakable Acts, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Speech and Silence
prompt: A theorist argues that some expression can silence others by affecting whether their words are recognized as meaningful contributions. Which answer best represents the course's treatment of this claim?
options: It treats subordination as a property of the message's content alone, like depicting a hierarchy.
It treats subordination as a downstream effect of expression, such as changing behavior after exposure.
It asks whether expression can act through social conventions, while separating that claim from legal restriction.
It takes the possibility of such an act to prove that lawmakers should restrict the expression.
hint: The reading separates conceptual possibility, empirical support, and policy conclusions.
explanation: The Langton session examines whether some expression can subordinate or silence through illocutionary acts, rather than only through content or downstream effects. It notes empirical assumptions remain and that even a true claim would not by itself prove legal restriction is justified.

source.title: Session 22: Langton on Speech Acts and Unspeakable Acts, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Should I Follow the Expert?
prompt: An independent scientist and a standards board both advise a researcher about a safety limit. The board's authority is defended on the ground that following it helps researchers better comply with reasons that already apply to them. Which account does this resemble?
options: An authority may be justified when following it helps people better act on reasons that already apply to them
An authority is justified whenever its rule has been accepted by most officials
An authority is justified when its commands replace every reason a person might have
An authority is justified only if its directives match each subject's existing preference
hint: The proposed authority is useful because it helps people act better on relevant reasons.
explanation: Raz's normal justification thesis says authority can be justified when subjects are more likely to conform to the reasons that apply to them by following the authority's directives than by deciding independently. This is a proposed test for legitimate authority, not a guarantee that any particular board deserves obedience.

source.title: Session 10: Raz, Authority and Justification, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: Obey or Decide for Yourself?
prompt: A political philosopher argues that if citizens have a moral duty to obey a ruler simply because the ruler commands, they may stop judging the reasons for their own actions. Which concern is this?
options: A concern that law is ineffective unless every citizen obeys every rule
Wolff's challenge that a general duty to obey may conflict with personal autonomy
Raz's claim that expertise can help people follow reasons that already apply to them
Hart's distinction between rules of recognition and rules of change
hint: The argument contrasts obedience based on authority with taking responsibility for one's own decisions.
explanation: Wolff argues that a duty to obey political authority simply because it commands could conflict with autonomy, understood as deciding in light of one's own assessment of reasons. The course notes also raise objections, such as whether following a rule or taking expert advice always sacrifices autonomy. This is a philosophical challenge, not a settled conclusion about political authority.

source.title: Session 7: Wolff, The Conflict Between Authority and Autonomy, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Open Sit-In
prompt: A group peacefully blocks entry, in breach of an obstruction law, to a government building. They act publicly, explain that a policy is unjust, and seek to change it. Under Rawls's definition used in the course, which feature most clearly fits civil disobedience?
options: A private refusal based on conscience, without a public appeal for legal change
A peaceful march that follows the law and asks officials to change a policy
A public, nonviolent, conscientious breach aimed at changing law or policy
A violent campaign that rejects the political community's shared procedures
hint: Rawls's definition includes purpose, publicity, and manner.
explanation: Rawls describes civil disobedience as a public, nonviolent, conscientious, politically motivated breach aimed at changing law or policy. The reading asks whether this definition is too narrow and what might justify such acts. Matching the definition does not by itself show that the protest is justified.

source.title: Session 11: Rawls, The Justification of Civil Disobedience, MIT OCW 24.235J Philosophy of Law, Spring 2012

title: The Unpopular Client
prompt: A defense lawyer believes a client probably committed the charged act, but the prosecution's case has not been tested. Which argument from the course offers a defense of vigorous representation without claiming that the client is innocent?
options: The client's probable guilt means the lawyer's personal duty is to withdraw from the case
The lawyer should use any tactic the client requests because the role replaces moral judgment
Vigorous defense can check state power without endorsing the client's alleged act
The lawyer's role settles the moral question because professional duties are always decisive
hint: Separate the lawyer's role in the system from personal endorsement, but keep the role's limits in view.
explanation: The course discusses role-differentiated duties and arguments from the value of the adversarial system: a strong defense can check state power, especially where liberty is at stake. The reading also examines concerns that the role can bracket ordinary moral considerations. This argument does not settle whether every lawyer should accept every client or what professional rules require in a real case.
